title: Vitruvius's three conditions of good building
description: Vitruvius's De architectura, the only complete architecture book to survive from antiquity, says good building needs firmness, commodity and delight.

facts.text: Vitruvius's De architectura, written between 33 and 14 BCE (about 2,000 years ago), is the only complete work on architecture to survive from classical antiquity.
Vitruvius named three principles of architecture, firmitas, utilitas and venustas; Henry Wotton's 1624 English version made them firmness, commodity and delight.
Firmness is structural strength, commodity is usefulness to the people who use the building, and delight is beauty.

title: What an architect does
description: An architect (from Greek 'chief builder') designs a building for a client and turns the design into drawings and specifications builders can price and build from, then guides approvals and can inspect the work.

facts.text: The word architect comes from Greek arkhitekton, 'master builder', from arkhi- ('chief') and tekton ('builder').
An architect helps a client prepare the brief, designs the building, and produces drawings with technical specifications that builders can price and build from.
An architect advises on approvals such as planning permission and building regulations and, as contract administrator, can inspect the work on site.

title: How building changed: a timeline
description: From sun-dried mud brick and post-and-lintel stone, through Roman concrete domes and Florence, to iron-and-glass and the steel skeleton.

facts.text: Sun-dried mud brick was one of the first building materials; bricks were first made in sun-dried form at least 6,000 years ago.
The post-and-lintel system was the basis of architecture from prehistoric to Roman times.
Rome's Pantheon was rebuilt by the emperor Hadrian between 118 and 128 CE, under a great concrete dome.
The dome of Florence Cathedral, designed by Filippo Brunelleschi, was begun in 1420 and completed in 1436.
London's Crystal Palace, built of prefabricated iron and glass, opened for the Great Exhibition in Hyde Park in 1851.
Chicago's Home Insurance Building (1884-85) is generally considered the first tall building held up by an iron and steel skeleton frame.

title: Dead loads and live loads
description: A building carries permanent dead loads (its own structure and fixed parts) and changing live loads (people, furniture, weather, wind).

facts.text: Dead loads act permanently: the self-weight of the structure plus things like roofing, flooring, pipes, ducts and partition walls.
Live loads are transient and can change: people, sofas, pianos, books and cars, plus loads from the weather; wind counts as a sideways (lateral) live load.

title: The load path
description: Every load needs a continuous route from where it is applied, through the structure and foundation, into the soil.

facts.text: A load path is the route a force takes through a structure; a continuous load path carries loads from the roof, through the walls, to the foundation and into the supporting soil.

title: Tension and compression
description: Compression pushes and squeezes; tension pulls and stretches. A post carrying weight is squeezed; a cable holding a hanging weight is stretched.

facts.text: Compression is a pushing, squeezing force and tension a pulling, stretching one; structures must resist both.
A cable holding up a hanging load is in tension, while a post or tower carrying weight down to the ground is in compression.

title: The post-and-lintel system
description: Two upright posts carry a horizontal lintel across their tops: the system of Stonehenge and of doors and windows today.

facts.text: In the post-and-lintel system, two upright posts hold up a horizontal lintel laid across their tops; Stonehenge was built on this system.
A beam spanning an opening such as a door or window, with brick or stone wall above it, is often called a lintel.
Stonehenge's lintels sit on the uprights with mortise-and-tenon joints and lock to each other with tongue-and-groove joints, usually found only in woodworking.

title: Why beams bend, and why stone beams stay short
description: A loaded beam is squeezed on top and stretched underneath; brittle stone is weak in tension, so stone lintels must be short and posts close together.

facts.text: When a beam bends under a load, its top is squeezed in compression and its bottom is stretched in tension.
Brick and stone are brittle and weak in tension, so they can provide only a short lintel.

title: How an arch works
description: Wedge-shaped voussoirs, locked by a keystone, are squeezed together by the load; built on centering, an arch of small blocks spans wider than a stone lintel.

facts.text: An arch is built of wedge-shaped blocks called voussoirs, each cut to press firmly against its neighbors; the central one is the keystone.
Weight pressing down on an arch forces its voussoirs together instead of apart, keeping the masonry in compression.
While an arch is being built, its voussoirs need support from below, usually temporary wooden centering, until the keystone is set.
Arches can span much wider openings than lintels because they are made of small, easily carried blocks rather than one massive stone.
The Romans used the semicircular arch in bridges, aqueducts and large-scale buildings.

title: An arch's thrust
description: An arch also pushes outward at its feet (thrust), so it needs massive supports to carry that push into the foundation.

facts.text: An arch's load produces a diagonal outward force called thrust, which will make the arch collapse unless its supports are massive enough to resist it and carry it into the foundation.

title: A dome: the arch turned in a circle
description: A dome evolved from the arch and pushes outward all around its rim, so large domes need heavy support.

facts.text: A dome is a hemispherical structure that evolved from the arch, usually forming a ceiling or roof.
A dome pushes outward all around its perimeter, so early large domes such as Rome's Pantheon needed heavy supporting walls.

title: A dome's hoop forces
description: Horizontal hoop forces let a dome rise ring by ring without centering; they squeeze near the top but turn to tension toward the base, where masonry domes crack into slices.

facts.text: Besides forces running down its curve, a dome carries hoop forces in horizontal rings; they let a dome be built ring by ring without centering, which an arch cannot do.
In a hemispherical dome, hoop forces squeeze near the top but turn to tension toward the base; masonry domes tend to crack along their meridians into slices whose bases lean outward.

title: Florence's dome and its tie rings
description: Florence Cathedral's dome (completed 1436) is still the largest masonry dome in the world; Brunelleschi bound it with tie rings of stone and oak.

facts.text: Florence Cathedral's dome, completed in 1436, is still the largest masonry dome in the world.
Brunelleschi built Florence's dome without formwork.
Brunelleschi bound Florence's dome with tie rings of stone held by metal cramps and of oak timbers joined by metal connectors.

title: Stone and wood: strengths and weaknesses
description: Stone is strong when squeezed and resists fire but is weak when stretched; wood is strong for its weight and spans farther but burns.

facts.text: Stone has great strength in compression but lacks tensile strength; masonry also resists fire.
Wood is strong in relation to its weight and relatively easy to work.
The Greeks substituted wooden beams for stone because wood required fewer supports and opened up interior spaces.
After the Great Fire of 1666, London changed from a city of wood into a city of brick, to gain protection from fire.

title: Mud brick and fired brick
description: The first bricks were sun-dried mud; firing in a kiln makes them strong and hard. Bricks were sized for one person to handle.

facts.text: Fired brick is burned in a kiln for strength, hardness and heat resistance; at Ur, potters discovered the closed kiln, whose heat could be controlled.
Ancient brickmakers held that a brick should be no larger than one person could easily handle.

title: Roman concrete
description: The Romans made concrete of lime, volcanic ash and rock; it set in seawater, and the Pantheon's dome is still the largest unreinforced concrete dome.

facts.text: Rome's Pantheon, rebuilt under Hadrian between 118 and 128 CE and almost 1,900 years old, still has the world's largest unreinforced concrete dome.
Roman builders made concrete by mixing lime with volcanic ash and chunks of volcanic rock.
Vitruvius recorded that the best marine concrete used volcanic ash from around the Gulf of Naples; Roman harbor structures have survived 2,000 years underwater.

title: Self-healing Roman concrete (2023 findings)
description: A 2023 MIT-led study found that lime clasts from hot mixing with quicklime can let Roman concrete seal its own cracks.

facts.text: A 2023 MIT-led study of Roman concrete from Privernum found that its white lime clasts, once blamed on poor mixing, formed when builders mixed in hot quicklime.
In the study, water reaching a clast through a crack dissolved calcium that refilled the crack as calcium carbonate; hot-mixed test samples sealed their cracks within two weeks.

title: Modern and reinforced concrete
description: Portland cement (1824) binds modern concrete; concrete is weak in tension, so steel bars take the stretch, an idea credited to Joseph Monier's 1867 patent.

facts.text: In 1824 the English inventor Joseph Aspdin burned and ground limestone and clay together to make portland cement, still the main binder in concrete.
Plain concrete resists compression well but not tension; in reinforced concrete, steel bars take the tension and the concrete takes the compression.
Reinforced concrete is usually credited to Joseph Monier, a Paris gardener who made concrete pots and tubs reinforced with iron mesh and patented it in 1867.

title: Load-bearing walls versus a frame
description: In a load-bearing building the walls carry the floors; in a frame building a skeleton of columns and beams does, so the outer wall bears only itself and can be light, even glass.

facts.text: In a load-bearing building the walls carry the floors above; the earliest skyscrapers rested on extremely thick masonry walls at ground level.
In a frame building, a skeleton of columns and beams carries the floors, and the outer wall bears only its own weight and hangs on the frame.

title: The Crystal Palace
description: A gardener's iron-and-glass building for 1851, sketched on blotting paper and built within six months from prefabricated parts.

facts.text: Joseph Paxton was superintendent of the gardens at Chatsworth from 1826 and built glasshouses there, including a lily house in 1850.
The Crystal Palace, built for the Great Exhibition of 1851 in Hyde Park, had slender iron rods holding up walls of clear glass.
Made of prefabricated parts of sheet glass and iron, the Crystal Palace was built within six months.
Paxton drew his first sketch of the Crystal Palace on blotting paper during a Midland Railway board meeting, following the lines of his Chatsworth lily house.

title: Why steel suits the frame
description: Unlike stone or brittle cast iron, steel has high tensile strength, so it handles the stretch in beams; an iron and steel skeleton held up the Home Insurance Building.

facts.text: Steel has high tensile strength, while cast iron is brittle and weak in tension.

title: Plans, sections, elevations and scale
description: A plan is a horizontal cut, a section a vertical cut, an elevation a face seen straight on; all are drawn to scale so builders can measure from them.

facts.text: A plan is a horizontal cut through a building, usually taken about three to four feet above the floor and seen from above.
A section is a vertical cut through a building; an elevation shows a vertical surface, such as the front of a building, seen straight on.
Architectural drawings are drawn to scale; at one half inch to one foot, each half inch on paper stands for a foot of building.
Within a week, Paxton's sketches were turned into proper drawings and presented to the exhibition's commission.

title: How blueprints were made
description: The cyanotype (1842) turned treated paper blue where light hit it, giving white lines on blue; it was used for copying drawings from the 1870s until diazo prints replaced it.

facts.text: John Herschel introduced the cyanotype, or blueprint, process in 1842, using paper treated with ferric ammonium citrate and potassium ferricyanide.
To make a blueprint, a drawing on translucent material is laid over the treated paper and exposed to light, giving white lines on a dark blue background.
Blueprints caught on for copying drawings in the 1870s, once commercial paper was sold; diazo prints had replaced them in most architectural offices by the 1950s.
The word blueprint is recorded from 1882, and its figurative sense, 'a detailed plan', from 1926.

title: Hooke's hanging chain
description: A hanging chain is in pure tension along its curve; turned upside down, the same shape stands as an arch in pure compression (Hooke, 1675).

facts.text: In 1675 Robert Hooke hid his finding in a Latin anagram: 'As hangs the flexible line, so but inverted will stand the rigid arch.'
A hanging chain is in tension along its curve; turned upside down, those forces become compression along the arch, so it does not bend or buckle.

title: Keeping the line of thrust inside the masonry
description: Engineers treat masonry as having no tensile strength; if a line of thrust fits entirely inside it, an arch or dome can be shown to be safe.

facts.text: Masonry is analyzed as having no tensile strength; if a line of thrust can be found lying entirely within the masonry, the structure can be shown to be safe for those loads.

title: Göbekli Tepe: a monument before farming
description: Hunter-gatherers raised Göbekli Tepe's pillar enclosures about 11,500 years ago; long read as a temple, it turns out people lived there too.

facts.text: Göbekli Tepe, in southeastern Turkey, was built by hunter-gatherers, before farming, beginning about 11,500 years ago.
Göbekli Tepe's T-shaped limestone pillars, set in round and oval enclosures, reach over 5 meters tall and weigh up to 50 tons.
Göbekli Tepe's first excavator, Klaus Schmidt, read it as a ritual center where people gathered but did not live.
Recent excavations at Göbekli Tepe found hearths, domestic buildings and a rainwater cistern cut into the bedrock, evidence that people lived there beside the great enclosures.

title: The first houses: Çatalhöyük and Skara Brae
description: Çatalhöyük packed mud-brick houses together with no streets, entered through the roof; Skara Brae kept its stone furniture for 5,000 years.

facts.text: Çatalhöyük, a Neolithic settlement in Turkey, has building periods from about 6700 BCE to about 5650 BCE; its people lived in rectangular mud-brick houses.
Çatalhöyük's houses were built close together with no streets in between; people moved around on the roofs and climbed down a wooden ladder through an opening in the ceiling.
Çatalhöyük's houses were repeatedly filled in and rebuilt on top of each other, eventually creating the mound seen today.
Skara Brae in Orkney, Scotland, about 5,000 years old, is the best-preserved Neolithic settlement in Western Europe; its houses keep stone dressers and box beds, and a storm uncovered it in 1850.

title: The ziggurat: a solid stepped temple tower
description: A ziggurat was a stepped temple tower of Mesopotamia with no rooms inside; at Ur, three staircases led to a temple on top.

facts.text: A ziggurat was a stepped temple tower of ancient Mesopotamia, usually square or rectangular, with no internal chambers; about 25 are known.
The ziggurat at Ur dates to about 2100 BCE, under King Ur-Nammu; three staircases led to a temple on its flat top.
The legendary Tower of Babel is popularly associated with the ziggurat of Marduk's great temple in Babylon.

title: The ziggurat's waterproof skin
description: A mud-brick core wrapped in baked brick mortared with bitumen; weeper holes let water evaporate from the core.

facts.text: Ziggurats had a core of mud brick and an exterior of baked brick; at Ur, several million sun-dried bricks formed the core, and the facing bricks were mortared with bitumen, a natural tar, to make a waterproof surface.
The Ur ziggurat's facing was punctuated by weeper holes that let water evaporate from the core.

title: Reed reinforcement in ziggurats
description: At Aqar Quf, layers of reed matting and plaited reed ropes run through the brickwork as reinforcement.

facts.text: At the Aqar Quf ziggurat in Iraq, a layer of reed matting bedded in sand and gravel lies after every eight or nine courses of bricks, and plaited reed ropes run through the structure from side to side as reinforcement.
Reed matting kept ziggurats from slumping to the side when they got wet.

title: The Great Pyramid's stones
description: Yellowish limestone core, finer limestone casing and passages, and a King's Chamber built, lined and roofed with granite.

facts.text: About 2.3 million stone blocks went into the Great Pyramid, a structure of some 5.75 million tons, completed about 4,500 years ago, in the early 25th century BCE.

The Great Pyramid's core is yellowish limestone blocks; the outer casing and inner passages are finer, light-colored limestone; the King's Chamber is built of huge granite blocks, lined and roofed with granite.

title: The Great Pyramid's relieving compartments
description: Five compartments above the King's Chamber, separated by granite slabs and topped by a gabled roof, probably shield its flat ceiling from the weight above.

facts.text: Above the King's Chamber are five compartments separated by massive horizontal granite slabs, probably built to shield the chamber's ceiling by diverting the thrust of the masonry above.
The topmost relieving compartment above the King's Chamber has a gabled roof of huge limestone blocks leaning against each other in pairs, which helps bear the weight above.

title: Karnak's Great Hypostyle Hall
description: A hypostyle hall's roof rests on columns: at Karnak, 134 of them under stone lintels, with a taller central aisle lit by clerestory grilles.

facts.text: Karnak's Great Hypostyle Hall covers nearly an acre; almost all of Paris's Notre-Dame cathedral could rest inside it.
A hypostyle hall is an interior space whose roof rests on pillars or columns; the word means literally 'under pillars.'
The interiors of Egyptian temples and the exteriors of Greek temples are lined with columns covered by stone lintels.
Karnak's Great Hypostyle Hall has 134 columns: 12 in the central nave about 20 m tall with open papyrus-flower capitals, and 122 shorter columns about 14 m tall with closed-bud capitals.
The Hypostyle Hall's only daylight came through huge stone window grilles in the clerestory beside the tall central columns; with its roof on, the hall stood in twilight even at midday.

title: The plan of an Egyptian temple
description: Pylon, open court, hypostyle hall and sanctuary: darker, more enclosed and higher toward the god, recreating the mound of creation.

facts.text: An Egyptian temple led from a pylon gateway to an open court, a hypostyle hall and the sanctuary holding the god's statue; the open court may have been as far as non-priests could go.

Papyrus-shaped columns in hypostyle halls evoked the marshes around the mound of creation; the sanctuary was the darkest, most enclosed part of the temple, with the highest floor, recreating that mound.

title: The Seven Wonders of the ancient world
description: Two tombs, two statues, a temple, gardens and a lighthouse, listed by Greek writers of the 2nd century BCE; only the pyramids survive.

facts.text: One of the best-known lists of the Seven Wonders was written by the Greek writer Antipater of Sidon in the 2nd century BCE.

The Seven Wonders of the ancient world were the Pyramids of Giza, the Hanging Gardens of Babylon, the Statue of Zeus at Olympia by Phidias, the Temple of Artemis at Ephesus, the Mausoleum of Halicarnassus, the Colossus of Rhodes and the Pharos (lighthouse) of Alexandria.
The Pyramids of Giza are the oldest of the Seven Wonders and the only one still substantially in existence.
The Mausoleum of Halicarnassus was built by Artemisia for her husband Mausolus, and the word mausoleum comes from it.

title: How six wonders were lost
description: Fire, earthquakes and stone recycling destroyed six wonders; the Hanging Gardens may never have been at Babylon at all.

facts.text: The Temple of Artemis at Ephesus was burned by Herostratus in 356 BCE, rebuilt, and later wrecked by invading Goths.
The Colossus of Rhodes, made of bronze plates fastened to an iron framework, was toppled by an earthquake about 226 BCE, little more than half a century after it was finished.
The Mausoleum of Halicarnassus was probably destroyed by an earthquake between the 11th and 15th centuries CE, and its stones were reused in local buildings.

Tradition says Nebuchadnezzar II built the Hanging Gardens of Babylon for his wife Amytis, who missed her homeland's mountains, but no certain trace has been found at Babylon; one theory places them at Nineveh, built by Sennacherib.

title: The Parthenon's refinements
description: A base that curves up, columns that swell (entasis) and lean inward, thicker corners: few straight lines, for reasons still debated.

facts.text: The Parthenon, Athena's temple in Athens, was designed by Ictinus and Callicrates and built from 447 BCE in about eight or nine years.

The Parthenon's base curves upward toward the middle, its columns swell slightly (entasis) and slope imperceptibly inward, its corner columns are slightly thicker, and it has few perfectly straight lines.
The refinements are classically explained as correcting optical illusions, such as a row of straight columns looking thinner in the middle, but that explanation is debated.

title: Building the Parthenon without mortar
description: Hand-trimmed marble blocks with near-invisible joints, locked by iron clamps sealed in lead; unleaded iron from 1898 cracked the marble, so restorers use titanium.

facts.text: The Parthenon was built without mortar, so every block had to be trimmed by hand; its joints are all but invisible, even under a magnifying glass.
The Parthenon's builders joined its marble blocks with iron clamps set in carved grooves and poured molten lead over them, sealing the iron.
From 1898, Nikolaos Balanos restored the Parthenon with iron clamps but no lead coating; rain swelled the iron and cracked the marble.
Today's Acropolis restorers replace the old iron clamps with titanium, which won't corrode and crack the marble.

title: How the Colosseum is built
description: A freestanding oval with a travertine framework, tufa and concrete, barrel and groin vaults, and three stories of arcades framed by the Greek orders.

facts.text: The Colosseum is a freestanding oval about 189 by 156 m that could hold as many as 50,000 spectators.
The Colosseum has a framework of travertine, with walls of tufa and concrete, and uses a complex system of barrel and groin vaults.
Three stories of the Colosseum are encircled by arcades framed by engaged columns in the Doric, Ionic and Corinthian orders.

title: Moving the Colosseum crowd
description: At least 80 entrances, 76 of them numbered to match tickets; class seating zones; vomitoria passages that disgorged the spectators.

facts.text: The Colosseum had no fewer than 80 entrances; 76 were numbered, and tickets were sold for each.
The Colosseum's seats were divided into zones by class, with wooden seats and standing room on the top tier for women and the poor.
A vomitorium is an entrance passage piercing the banks of seats of a theater, amphitheater or stadium; the name comes from Latin vomere, 'to vomit', for the way it disgorged the spectators.

title: Keeping an aqueduct flowing downhill
description: Gravity-fed aqueducts had to hold a gentle slope (about 25 cm per km at Nîmes); they ran mostly underground, crossing valleys on arches like the Pont du Gard.

facts.text: The Roman aqueduct serving Nîmes ran about 50 km, and its average gradient is estimated at only about 25 to 34 cm per kilometer (sources differ).
Roman aqueducts moved water by gravity alone, so they had to maintain their gradients over varied terrain.
Of about 420 km of aqueducts serving Rome, only about 50 km crossed valleys on stone arches; the rest were underground conduits.
The Pont du Gard carried the Nîmes aqueduct across the Gard River on three tiers of arches, with the water channel on top, and was built without mortar.

title: Surveying a level: the chorobates
description: Vitruvius's chorobates: a twenty-foot straightedge on legs whose plumb lines, or water in a groove, show level.

facts.text: Vitruvius described the chorobates, a leveling instrument: a straightedge about twenty feet long on two legs, with plumb lines that show it stands level when they match marked lines.
If wind disturbed the chorobates' plumb lines, water poured into a groove along its top showed the level instead.

title: Lightening the Pantheon
description: Materials graded from heavy basalt below to pumice at the top of the vault, over walls 6 m thick braced by brick arches.

facts.text: The Pantheon's dome is about 43 m in diameter.
The Pantheon's materials are graded by height, from heavy basalt in the foundations, through brick and tufa, to the lightest pumice toward the center of the vault.
The Pantheon's walls are 6 m thick, and its drum is strengthened by huge brick arches and piers set one above another inside the walls.

title: The Pantheon's cracked dome
description: Meridional cracks split the lower dome into slices that work as arches sharing the uncracked upper dome as keystone (Mark and Hutchinson, 1986).

facts.text: The Pantheon's dome has cracks running top to rim through its lower half; they stop short of the oculus, the round opening at the top. Robert Mark and Paul Hutchinson analyzed this in 1986.
In Mark and Hutchinson's analysis, the Pantheon's cracked lower dome acts as a series of arches sharing the uncracked upper dome, around the oculus, as a common keystone.

title: Trabeated and arcuated building
description: Trabeated building uses beams or lintels (Egypt, Greece); arcuated building uses arches (Rome).

facts.text: Trabeated means designed or constructed with horizontal beams or lintels.
In architecture, arcuated means having arches.

title: Hagia Sophia's pendentives
description: Hagia Sophia (532-537) sets a round dome over a square using pendentives, curved triangles that gather the dome's weight onto four piers.

facts.text: Hagia Sophia was built for Justinian between 532 and 537 by Anthemius of Tralles, an architect and mathematician, and Isidorus of Miletus, a professor of physics.
A pendentive is a curved triangle of masonry filling an upper corner of a square room so that the tops form a circular support for a dome; Hagia Sophia is an early, large example.
At Hagia Sophia, two pairs of arches meet on pendentives that carry the dome's load down through four massive piers.

title: Hagia Sophia's windows and half domes
description: 40 windows at the dome's base make it seem suspended, while two half domes east and west act as buttresses against its outward push.

facts.text: Forty windows ring the base of Hagia Sophia's dome, making it seem almost suspended above the space.
At Hagia Sophia, two giant half domes on the east and west join the arches under the main dome and extend the covered space lengthwise.
A half dome is often used as a buttress at the base of a larger dome, as at Hagia Sophia.

title: Hagia Sophia's rebuilt, taller dome
description: Part of the first, too-shallow dome fell in 558; Isidorus the Younger raised the new dome's crown by about 6 m to reduce its thrust, finishing in 562.

facts.text: After an earthquake, part of Hagia Sophia's first dome collapsed in 558; ASCE's account blames its shallow shape, which loaded the walls instead of the piers.
Isidorus the Younger rebuilt Hagia Sophia's dome by 562, raising its crown about 6 meters (20.5 ft) to reduce its sideways thrust, and adding 40 ribs.

title: The qibla, mihrab, minbar and minaret
description: A mosque is built around the qibla, the direction of Mecca, marked by the mihrab; the minbar is a pulpit and the minaret is for the call to prayer.

facts.text: In a mosque, the mihrab, a niche for the imam who leads the prayer, points to the qibla, the direction of Mecca that Muslims face in prayer.
A mosque's minbar is a pulpit of steps for the preacher; from the minaret, the muezzin gives the call to prayer five times each day.

title: How Córdoba's Great Mosque grew
description: Córdoba's prayer hall of rows of columns (784-786) was extended by moving its qibla wall; 9th- and 10th-century extensions doubled it to some 850 columns.

facts.text: The Great Mosque of Córdoba was built by the Umayyad ruler Abd al-Rahman I in 784-786; extensions in the 9th and 10th centuries doubled its size.
Some 850 pillars carry the roof of Córdoba's former mosque, in rows supporting two tiers of arches.
When Córdoba's population grew, Abd al-Rahman II extended the prayer hall southward, demolishing the original qibla wall and building a new one.

title: Sinan and the Süleymaniye
description: Sinan, Ottoman chief architect for about 40 years, based the Süleymaniye (1550-1557) on Hagia Sophia and planned it around its central dome.

facts.text: Sinan worked as chief architect of the Ottoman Empire for about the last 40 years of his life.
Sinan built the Süleymaniye Mosque in Istanbul for Sultan Süleyman in 1550-1557, basing it on the design of Hagia Sophia.
In Sinan's mosques the huge central dome became the focal point around which the rest of the design was developed, with smaller domes and buttresses leading up to it.

title: The Romanesque barrel vault and thick walls
description: A barrel vault is a row of arches; it pushes outward along its whole length, so Romanesque churches needed massive walls with few windows.

facts.text: Romanesque churches used semicircular arches, barrel or groin vaults, and massive piers and walls with few windows to contain the outward thrust of the vaults.
A barrel vault is in effect a continuous series of arches; it thrusts like an arch and must be buttressed along its entire length by heavy walls with limited openings.

title: The groin vault
description: Two barrel vaults crossing at right angles make a groin vault, whose thrust gathers at four corners.

facts.text: Two barrel vaults crossing at right angles form a groin vault; in a row, groin vaults can cover long rectangular spaces, and their thrust gathers at the four corners, so only those points need buttressing.

title: Durham Cathedral's rib vaults
description: Durham Cathedral (begun 1093) is the earliest known example of stone ribs forming pointed arches under a vault; the ribs allow thinner, lighter filling.

facts.text: Durham Cathedral in England, begun in 1093, is an outstanding example of Romanesque architecture.
Durham Cathedral is the earliest known example of stone ribs forming pointed arches to support a vault; the ribs let the filling be thinner and lighter, and the vault has stood for 900 years.

title: Why Gothic builders used the pointed arch
description: Unlike a round arch, a pointed arch can be made to rise to the same height over different spans, so vault ribs meet neatly; Saint-Denis (about 1135-44) combined it with the rib vault.

facts.text: The abbey church of Saint-Denis, rebuilt about 1135 to 1144, was one of the earliest buildings to combine the rib vault, flying buttress and pointed arch into a coherent Gothic style.
Pointed arches escape the rigid geometry of semicircular arches, whose height is set by their width: arches of different spans can rise to the same height.
Skilled use of the pointed arch and the ribbed vault let Gothic builders cover far more elaborate and complicated ground plans than before.

title: The flying buttress
description: A half arch that carries a vault's thrust from the upper wall across an aisle to an outer pier, often weighted by a pinnacle.

facts.text: A flying buttress is a half arch that carries the thrust of a roof or vault from the upper part of a wall across an aisle to an outer pier.
A pinnacle often tops the pier of a flying buttress, adding weight and stability; the flying buttress evolved from simpler hidden supports and made high-ceilinged Gothic churches possible.

title: Gothic walls of glass
description: With ribs, piers and buttresses carrying the vault, Gothic walls opened into large windows; Chartres (after 1194) enlarged its clerestory.

facts.text: Gothic builders used the pointed arch, rib vault and flying buttress to build taller and to open up the wall between supports for larger windows.

At Chartres Cathedral, mainly built after 1194, the architect dropped the gallery level and used specially designed flying buttresses to enlarge the clerestory; great churches after it were dominated by glass set high up.
A clerestory is a wall with windows carried higher than the surrounding roofs to light the interior.

title: Plate tracery and bar tracery
description: Plate tracery cut openings through a stone slab; bar tracery (after 1220, early at Reims) used thin stone bars, so windows held more glass.

facts.text: Early Gothic windows used plate tracery, openings cut through a slab of stone, as at 12th-century Chartres.
Bar tracery, developed after 1220, divides a window with thin upright stone bars; early examples are at Reims Cathedral, before 1230.

title: Iron hidden in Gothic walls
description: Notre-Dame de Paris (iron staples from the 1160s) is the first known Gothic cathedral to use iron massively; mid-13th-century builders embedded iron chains in wall tops.

facts.text: A 2023 study, made possible by the 2019 fire, dated iron staples in Notre-Dame's galleries to about the 1160s: the first known Gothic cathedral to use iron massively as a building material.
By the mid-13th century, Gothic builders embedded iron chain links at the tops of walls, as in the Sainte-Chapelle.

title: Angkor Wat as Mount Meru
description: Suryavarman II's 12th-century temple to Vishnu models the Hindu cosmos: five towers for Meru's peaks, a moat for the oceans.

facts.text: Angkor Wat was built in the 12th century by the Khmer king Suryavarman II and dedicated to the Hindu god Vishnu.
Angkor Wat's five central towers symbolize the peaks of Mount Meru, the sacred mountain of Hindu cosmology.
Angkor Wat's enormous moat, about 200 meters wide, suggests the oceans at the edge of the world.
Angkor Wat appears on the Cambodian flag, and Britannica calls it the world's largest religious structure, covering some 400 acres.

title: Angkor, a capital built around water
description: Angkor, the Khmer capital from the 9th to the 15th century, had a vast system of reservoirs, canals and moats.

facts.text: Angkor was the capital of the Khmer Empire from the 9th to the 15th century.
One of Angkor's most notable features was a vast system of reservoirs, canals and moats, used for irrigation and also symbolizing the cosmic waters.

title: How Angkor's stone arrived
description: Angkor Wat is laterite cased in Kulen Hills sandstone; a 2012 study traced a canal route from the quarries much shorter than the overland one.

facts.text: Angkor Wat is built on laterite encased in sandstone quarried in the Kulen Hills.

In 2012, Waseda University researchers Etsuo Uchida and Ichita Shimoda used satellite images to trace canals from more than 50 quarries at the foot of Mount Kulen to Angkor, a route less than half as long as the overland one once assumed.

title: The pagoda, from the stupa
description: The pagoda grew out of the Indian stupa, built to hold relics; five-story pagodas reached Japan in the 6th century, and Hōryū-ji's was rebuilt about 711.

facts.text: The pagoda derives from the stupa, a domed monument first built in ancient India to house relics; five-story pagodas were built to enshrine remains of the Buddha.
The five-story pagoda reached Japan from India by way of China, with Buddhism, in the 6th century.
The five-story pagoda of Hōryū-ji, in Nara, was rebuilt around 711 after a fire and is regarded as the oldest existing wooden pagoda in Japan.

title: Why pagodas ride out earthquakes
description: Hōryū-ji's stories are independent frames, its ground columns untied, and its wooden joints can rub and slide; no five-story pagoda is recorded as toppling in an earthquake.

facts.text: Engineers studying the Hōryū-ji pagoda found no historical record of a five-story pagoda toppling in an earthquake, and no serious damage to old wooden pagodas was reported after the 1995 Kobe earthquake.
In the Hōryū-ji pagoda each story is an independent framework with no column tying them together, and the first-story columns are not tied down to the foundation.
Researchers credit pagodas' earthquake resistance to friction and sliding in their many wooden joints and the balancing-toy effect of their deep eaves, among other factors.

title: The shinbashira
description: The pagoda's central column (shinbashira) at Hōryū-ji carries only the top spire; it keeps the roofs from sliding far in a quake.

facts.text: At Hōryū-ji, the central column, the shinbashira, supports only the ornamental spire on top, independently of the main structure.
One explanation of the central pole: when a quake makes the heavy roofs try to slide sideways, the pole won't let any roof move very far.

title: The garbhagriha
description: The heart of a Hindu temple is the garbhagriha, the small innermost sanctuary housing the deity's image or emblem, under the main tower.

facts.text: The garbhagriha, often translated "womb house", is the innermost and most sacred sanctuary of a Hindu temple, housing the main image or emblem of its deity.
Over the small sanctuary rises the temple's tower: a shikhara in northern India, a pyramidal vimana in the south.

title: The temple tower as a mountain
description: The Kandariya Mahadeva Temple (11th century, for Shiva) rises like a mountain range, referring to Mount Meru.

facts.text: The Kandariya Mahadeva Temple at Khajuraho, built in the 11th century, is dedicated to Shiva, represented by a linga in the womb chamber at its heart.
The Kandariya Mahadeva Temple's steeply rising, mountain-like form refers to Mount Meru, the mythical source of creation, and many miniature shrines on its spire add to the upward movement.

title: Northern and southern temple towers
description: Northern (Nagara) towers curve; southern (Dravida) vimanas are pyramids of receding stories, as at Thanjavur (1003-1010); later southern gateways (gopuras) grew huge.

facts.text: In northern (Nagara) Hindu temples the shikhara is usually curved in outline, and smaller towers often top the halls in front.
In southern (Dravida) temples the tower over the sanctuary is a pyramid of gradually receding stories; by the Vijayanagar period, gateways called gopuras had grown to dominate the temples inside.
The Brihadishvara Temple at Thanjavur, built in 1003-1010 under Rajaraja I, has a pyramidal vimana more than 60 meters high.

title: Rebuilding St. Peter's
description: St. Peter's replaced Constantine's basilica: begun 1506 (Bramante), Michelangelo from 1546, dome finished 1590, Maderno's Latin cross, consecrated 1626.

facts.text: Constantine ordered a basilica built on the site of Saint Peter's tomb in 315, and it was consecrated in 326.
Pope Julius II laid the first stone of the new St. Peter's in 1506, to Donato Bramante's Greek-cross plan (four equal arms) with a large central vault.
In 1546 Pope Paul III made the aged Michelangelo chief architect of St. Peter's; he kept a Greek cross and designed a new dome as the dominant element of the whole building.
St. Peter's dome, modified from Michelangelo's design, was completed under Giacomo della Porta by 1590.
From 1605 Carlo Maderno lengthened St. Peter's nave into a Latin cross, making it 187 meters (615 ft) long; Urban VIII consecrated the basilica in 1626, 120 years after its first stone.
According to Britannica, St. Peter's was the largest church in the world until 1989, when a basilica in Yamoussoukro, Côte d'Ivoire, exceeded it.

title: Poleni, the hanging chain and St. Peter's dome
description: In 1743 St. Peter's dome was cracking; Poleni showed with a weighted hanging chain (1748) that it was safe, and iron rings were fitted by 1748.

facts.text: In 1743 Pope Benedict XIV summoned the mathematician Giovanni Poleni to Rome because the dome of St. Peter's seemed near to collapsing.

In 1748 Poleni used Hooke's hanging chain to assess the cracked dome: he divided it into slices, hung 32 unequal weights matching each part, and showed the chain's curve fit within the masonry, so the dome was safe.
With the architect Luigi Vanvitelli, Poleni proposed fitting large iron rings to strengthen St. Peter's dome; the rings were fitted by 1748.

title: Which way holy buildings face
description: Orientation is a building's position on the east-west axis: churches usually put the altar east (Old St. Peter's faced west), mosques face Mecca, and Angkor Wat faces west.

facts.text: Orientation, from Latin oriens ("the rising sun"), is a building's position in relation to an east-west axis.
Christian churches have usually been oriented with the apse or high altar at the east end; Rome's Old St. Peter's basilica faced west instead.
Unlike the other temples around it, which face east, Angkor Wat faces west.

title: Castles: homes designed for defense
description: A castle was a lord's or king's home built to be attacked: towers project so defenders can shoot along the wall, and machicolations let them drop missiles straight down.

facts.text: A castle was a medieval stronghold, generally the residence of the king or lord of the territory around it.
Towers protruding from a castle wall let defenders bring flanking fire along the face and foot of the wall, and were built higher than the wall for extra range.
Wooden hoardings gave way to machicolations: permanent overhanging stone galleries with openings through which defenders dropped missiles on attackers directly below.

title: Mining: attacking a castle from underneath
description: Attackers dug a tunnel under a wall, propped it with timber and burned the props, bringing the masonry down, as King John did at Rochester in 1215.

facts.text: Mining meant digging a tunnel beneath a castle wall, holding it up with wooden props, then burning the props so the masonry above collapsed.
During King John's siege of Rochester Castle in 1215, miners attacked the keep's south-east turret, burning the fat of 40 pigs to fire the props and bring that corner down.
Rochester Castle's keep is the tallest such building to survive in Europe.

title: Why castle towers turned round
description: Square towers and keeps were vulnerable to mining at their corners, so castle towers became round; Rochester rebuilt its lost corner semicircular.

facts.text: Rectangular keeps could be undermined quite easily: a tunnel dug under a corner, filled with wood and set alight, made the tower partly collapse.
Castle towers projecting from the walls were square at first but later round, and many rectangular keeps were replaced with circular ones, less vulnerable to undermining.
Rochester's square south-east turret, destroyed in the 1215 siege, was rebuilt as a semicircular tower.

title: The Great Wall: built over centuries
description: Not one wall: Qin Shi Huang joined older border walls around 220 BCE, and the Ming (1368-1644) built the most extensive, best-preserved version.

facts.text: The Great Wall was built by a series of governments over about 2,000 years; it is not one long, unbroken wall.
Around 220 BCE, Qin Shi Huang, the first emperor of a unified China, had existing border walls joined into one; at that time rammed earth and wood made up most of the wall.
The most extensive and best-preserved version of the Great Wall dates from the Ming dynasty (1368-1644), whose emperors added watchtowers and platforms; most familiar photos show Ming work.
All sections of the Great Wall ever built add up to about 21,196 km.

title: The Great Wall: many materials
description: The wall used rammed earth, brick, granite and marble in different places, and the Ming bound bricks with lime mortar containing sticky rice.

facts.text: The Great Wall is made of different materials in different places: rammed earth (hard-packed soil) in some, brick in others, and quarried granite or even marble blocks elsewhere.
Researchers at Zhejiang University found that Ming builders of the Great Wall added sticky rice to their lime mortar.

title: The Great Wall from space: a myth
description: The wall looks like the stone and soil around it, so it is hard to see even from low Earth orbit; NASA says it is not visible from the Moon.

facts.text: NASA says the Great Wall isn't visible from the Moon and is difficult or impossible to see from Earth orbit without high-powered lenses.
Because the Great Wall looks a lot like the stone and soil around it, it is difficult to make out with the human eye even from low Earth orbit.

title: The word palace and Rome's Palatine Hill
description: Palace comes from Rome's Palatine Hill, where Augustus's house stood and Nero later built a splendid residence.

facts.text: The word palace derives from Rome's Palatine Hill, where the emperors built their residences.
Augustus's house stood on the Palatine Hill, which later became the site of the splendid residence built by Nero.

title: What a palace is for
description: A palace is a royal residence that is sometimes also a seat of government or a religious centre; in Rome and Constantinople palaces were centres of power.

facts.text: A palace is a royal residence, and sometimes also a seat of government or a religious centre.
In Rome and Constantinople, palaces reached their peak as centres of power.

title: Two ways to plan a palace
description: After the Middle Ages, Western European palaces tended to be single buildings; East Asian palaces are many low, decorated wooden pavilions in vast walled gardens.

facts.text: In Western Europe after the Middle Ages, palaces tended to be single buildings.
East Asian palaces, such as Beijing's Forbidden City, consist of many buildings, mostly low, highly decorated wooden pavilions, within vast walled gardens.

title: The Forbidden City: who built it and why forbidden
description: Commissioned by the Yongle emperor in 1406 and occupied in 1420, it barred most subjects for five centuries and became the Palace Museum in 1925.

facts.text: The Forbidden City was commissioned in 1406 by the Yongle emperor of the Ming dynasty and first officially occupied by the court in 1420.
It was called the Forbidden City because access was barred to most of the subjects of the realm.
The Forbidden City was the centre of Chinese power for five centuries; Puyi, the last Qing emperor, left in 1924, and the Palace Museum was established there in 1925.

title: The Forbidden City: a plan that ranks
description: Behind a wall and moat, buildings line a north-south axis facing south; the Outer Court held government halls on marble terraces, the Inner Court the living quarters.

facts.text: The Forbidden City is surrounded by a high wall and a moat about 52 m (170 feet) wide.
The Forbidden City's most important buildings, especially those on its main north-south axis, face south to honour the Sun.
The Palace Museum says each Forbidden City structure followed the traditional Chinese architectural hierarchy and was designed to reflect imperial power.
In the Outer Court, three main halls of government stand on a three-tiered marble terrace above an immense plaza; the Inner Court held the imperial living quarters.
The Hall of Supreme Harmony, which holds the emperor's throne, is the largest single building in the Forbidden City.

title: The Forbidden City: timber post-and-lintel halls
description: Its halls are timber buildings with post-and-lintel frames under tiled roofs.

facts.text: Buildings in the Forbidden City feature timber construction, post-and-lintel frames and tiled roofs.

title: The Alhambra: fortress outside, palace inside
description: Built chiefly 1238-1358 by the Nasrids, its plain rammed-earth fortress walls ('the red') hide ornate rooms and patios.

facts.text: The Alhambra, on a plateau overlooking Granada, was built chiefly between 1238 and 1358 by Ibn al-Ahmar, founder of the Nasrid dynasty, and his successors.
The Alhambra's highly ornate interiors and patios contrast with the plain walls of its fortress exterior.
The name Alhambra means 'the red' in Arabic, probably after the reddish rammed earth of its outer walls.

title: The Alhambra: courtyards and water
description: Rooms open onto courtyards like the Court of the Myrtles and its reflecting pool; a royal canal brought river water to the hill.

facts.text: A dark, winding passage leads into the Court of the Myrtles, centred on a large reflecting pool set in marble paving, in which the palace is reflected.
The Alhambra's Royal Canal (Acequia Real) took water from the Darro river 11 km upstream, and it made the hill habitable.
The Nasrids brought the sound, sight and cooling of water into gardens, courtyards, marble canals and even indoors.

title: The Alhambra: tiles and carved plaster
description: Tiles cover the lower walls; above them, carved stucco runs in bands of curving patterns and calligraphy, once brightly painted.

facts.text: In the Alhambra's rooms, geometric tiles cover the lower walls, and the surfaces above are carved stucco (plaster) in bands and panels of curving patterns and calligraphy.
The carved stucco of the Comares facade was once painted in brilliant colours; only traces remain.

title: The Taj Mahal: who built it, for whom
description: Shah Jahan built it as a tomb for Mumtaz Mahal (died 1631) from about 1632, with 20,000+ workers; some famous stories about it are legends.

facts.text: The Mughal emperor Shah Jahan built the Taj Mahal as a tomb for his wife Mumtaz Mahal, who died in childbirth in 1631; both their cenotaphs are in its central chamber.
Building began about 1632, the mausoleum was finished by about 1638-39, and work on the whole complex spanned 22 years.
More than 20,000 workers from India, Persia, the Ottoman Empire and Europe built the Taj Mahal; its chief architect was probably Ustad Ahmad Lahawri.
Historians have found no evidence for the story that Shah Jahan had the builders' hands cut off, and some dismiss the idea of a black marble twin across the river.

title: The Taj Mahal: symmetry, minarets and inlay
description: Four matching facades, a twin building for balance, outward-leaning minarets, and semiprecious stones inlaid in white marble.

facts.text: The mausoleum has four nearly identical facades, a central dome about 73 m high ringed by four smaller domes, and a minaret at each corner.
Two identical red sandstone buildings flank the tomb: a mosque, and its twin, the jawab, which balances it.
The Taj Mahal's minarets lean slightly outward, so in a disaster such as an earthquake they would fall away from the tomb.
The Taj Mahal's white marble is decorated with pietra dura (Italian for 'hard stone'): semiprecious stones such as lapis lazuli, jade and turquoise inlaid in geometric and floral designs.

title: Versailles: a palace to control a court
description: A hunting lodge turned by Louis XIV into an immense palace; from 1682 it housed the whole court, keeping the nobility under the king's eye.

facts.text: Versailles began as a hunting lodge for Louis XIII in the 1620s; Louis XIV transformed it between 1661 and 1710 into an immense complex.
From 1682 Versailles was the official royal residence, with enough room to house the whole court.
Under the king's watchful eye at Versailles, the nobility could no longer plot against the throne; the great lords were kept eager to serve and please him.

title: The Hall of Mirrors
description: Built 1678-1684 by Hardouin-Mansart: 357 mirrors on 17 arches facing 17 windows, a boast of French wealth when mirrors were a luxury.

facts.text: Jules Hardouin-Mansart built the Hall of Mirrors from 1678 to 1684, replacing a terrace by Louis Le Vau that opened onto the garden.
The Hall of Mirrors, more than 70 m long, has 357 mirrors on 17 arches facing 17 windows.
Charles Le Brun painted 30 compositions on the Hall of Mirrors' vaulted ceiling, telling the story of Louis XIV's reign.
Mirrors were then a great luxury, and the hall showed that France's new mirror manufacture could rival Venice's monopoly; courtiers crossed it daily.

title: Machu Picchu: walls without mortar
description: An Inca estate, probably for Pachacuti, whose main walls are blocks fitted almost perfectly and held together by gravity, not mortar.

facts.text: Machu Picchu was probably built in the mid-15th century as a palace estate for the Inca ruler Pachacuti.
Machu Picchu's main walls are held together by gravity, not mortar: their blocks are joined almost perfectly beside and on top of each other.
Inca builders shaped some large polygonal blocks exactly for their places in a wall; a famous stone in Cusco has 12 sides.
The Inca knew mortar: a few small structures at Machu Picchu use it, but the largest walls are built completely without it.

title: Machu Picchu: walls that ride out earthquakes
description: Interlocking blocks can move in place, which is suggested to make the walls tougher in earthquakes; the evidence is anecdotal.

facts.text: Yale archaeologist Richard Burger says that when an earthquake hits Machu Picchu, only the modern restorations fall.
Machu Picchu's walls are thousands of interlocking, irregular blocks; it is suggested this makes them more earthquake-resistant because the stones can move in place.
In a massive earthquake in 1650, many Spanish colonial buildings in Cusco collapsed, while the Inca walls there and at Machu Picchu were unharmed.
Architectural historian Stella Nair notes that the evidence that Inca buildings endure earthquakes is anecdotal, without actual seismic research.

title: Machu Picchu: the hidden half
description: Kenneth Wright estimates 50-60 percent of the building effort went underground into foundations, site preparation and drainage.

facts.text: Engineer Kenneth Wright estimates the Inca spent about 50 to 60 percent of their building effort at Machu Picchu underground, on foundations and site preparation.

Under the main plaza, Wright found topsoil over sandy gravel over a drainage layer of granite waste rock from stone cutting; about 76 inches of rain fall a year, and without good drainage there would be no Machu Picchu.

title: Neuschwanstein: a knight's castle from a stage set
description: Begun 1869 for Ludwig II, it copies no real castle: stage-set designs mixing the Wartburg with book illustrations, a style called historicism.

facts.text: Neuschwanstein was built for King Ludwig II of Bavaria; its foundation stone was laid on 5 September 1869.
Ludwig II wrote to Richard Wagner, whom he greatly admired, that he meant to build 'in the authentic style of the old German knights' castles'.
Neuschwanstein's designs came from stage sets by the Munich scene painter Christian Jank, turned into plans by the architect Eduard Riedel.
Neuschwanstein copies no existing building: it is an example of historicism, combining motifs from the Wartburg with castles from medieval book illustrations.
After Bavaria lost a war to Prussia in 1866, Ludwig II was no longer a sovereign ruler; from 1867 he planned castles and palaces where he could be a real king.
Ludwig's father, Maximilian II, had the ruined castle of Hohenschwangau nearby rebuilt in the 'Gothic style' from 1832.

title: Neuschwanstein: modern technology in medieval guise
description: Brick walls clad in limestone, a steel Throne Hall, central heating, running water, electric bells and telephones; a retreat opened to the public after 1886.

facts.text: Neuschwanstein's walls are brick with light limestone used only as cladding, and its Throne Hall was built as an encased steel construction.
Neuschwanstein had hot-air central heating, running water on every floor, automatically flushing toilets, electric bells to call servants, and telephones on two floors.
Ludwig II built Neuschwanstein to withdraw from public life; it was unfinished when he died in 1886 and opened to the public within weeks.

title: Guns end the age of castles
description: French guns took castle after castle in Italy in 1494, ending the medieval castle; defense moved to modern fortification.

facts.text: When French troops marched through Italy in 1494, their guns reduced castle after castle with astonishing speed.
With firearms, the age of the medieval castle came to an end and the era of modern military fortification began.

title: From defense to comfort and display
description: Late castles added more rooms and big windows on inner courtyards; under the Tudors, English barons stopped building castles and moved into country houses.

facts.text: As medieval households grew and lords wanted more privacy, they built larger ranges of rooms inside their castles.
At castles like Bodiam, buildings were set around a central courtyard with a tower at each corner, so their inner faces could risk large windows.
Under the strong central rule of the Tudors, barons in England stopped building castles and moved into country houses.

title: Vitruvius: climate decides the style of a house
description: Vitruvius taught that a house must suit its climate: sheltered and closed in the cold north, open and turned away from the sun in the hot south.

facts.text: Vitruvius opened Book VI of De architectura with climate as what determines the style of a house: one style suits Egypt, another Spain, another Pontus, another Rome.

Vitruvius advised that in the north houses be roofed over and sheltered as much as possible, facing a warm exposure, and in hot southern countries be built more in the open, facing north or north-east.
In Morgan's translation, Vitruvius says designing for climate lets us 'amend by art what nature, if left to herself, would mar.'

title: Pitched roofs and flat roofs
description: Sloped roofs shed rain; flat roofs are traditional where the climate is arid.

facts.text: The earliest roofs were probably thatched with straw, leaves, branches or reeds, and were usually set at a slope, or pitch, so rainfall could drain off them.
Flat roofs have historically been widely used in the Middle East, the American Southwest and anywhere the climate is arid, where draining water off the roof matters less.

title: Vernacular building
description: ICOMOS defines vernacular building as the traditional and natural way communities house themselves, with skills passed on informally.

facts.text: ICOMOS's 1999 Charter on the Built Vernacular Heritage calls vernacular building the traditional and natural way by which communities house themselves.
The charter says vernacular building can be recognized by a manner of building shared by the community, a local character that responds to the environment, and expertise passed on informally.

title: The Inuit snow house
description: Iglu means house in Inuktitut. Inuit builders cut blocks of hard snow and lay them in an inward-leaning spiral that closes into a dome.

facts.text: Iglu means 'house' in Inuktitut; the snow iglu, or igloo, was a winter home and hunting-ground dwelling of Inuit in Canada and Greenland.
An experienced Inuit builder can build a snow igloo in one to two hours.
Igloo builders use knives of whalebone or metal to cut large blocks of hard snow, which form inward-leaning walls built in a spiral from inside.
The top surfaces of the first ring of blocks are shaved at a slope to form the first rung of a spiral; more blocks follow the spiral inward until the dome is complete.

title: Why an igloo stays warm
description: Hard-packed snow insulates better than ice, tiered floors put sleepers in the warmest air, and a lamp and body heat do the rest.

facts.text: The hard snow walls of an igloo are good insulators that keep in body heat and the heat of oil lamps (qulliq); solid ice holds heat less well than compressed snow.
Some igloos have tiered floors so that people can sleep above the lowest level, where it is warmer.
Warmth inside and cold Arctic air outside strengthen an igloo, because any thawing sections freeze again.
Temperatures inside an igloo are often just above freezing, but can reach about 15 degrees C, depending on how many people are inside and whether an oil lamp burns.
Inuit traditionally kept their fur-lined clothes on inside the igloo by day, and the oil lamp was the centre of social life, where people cooked, ate, warmed up and talked.

title: The Mongol ger, a portable home
description: The ger is a round, felt-covered wooden home that Mongolian herding families take down, carry and put up again.

facts.text: The Mongol ger is light enough for nomads to carry, flexible enough to fold and pack, and sturdy enough to be dismantled and reassembled.
A yurt is pitched wherever the nomad finds good pasture for the herds and is carried from place to place on horseback or on a small wagon.
A ger is a round structure of walls, poles and a peaked roof on a painted wooden frame, covered with white felt and canvas and tightened with ropes of animal hair.
The felt cover suits the cold, dry steppes, and nomads add extra layers of felt when the temperature drops.
The ger can withstand Mongolia's fierce spring winds.
The Mongolian word ger simply means 'dwelling'; in the West, yurt has become the common word for the round nomad homes of Central Asia, including the Mongolian ger.
Taking down and putting up a ger is always a family operation, and children learn by watching their elders.
Men carve the ger's wood while women and men paint, sew, stitch and make felt; cutting wool and making felt are usually communal work.
In 2013, UNESCO inscribed the traditional craftsmanship of the Mongol ger on its Representative List of the Intangible Cultural Heritage of Humanity.

title: A yurt roof: compression ring and tension band
description: Yurt roof poles meet in a center ring held in compression; their outward thrust at the wall is held by a tension band, so the roof can span without inner supports.

facts.text: In a yurt, the roof poles meet in a center ring, which holds them in a state of compression.
Where a yurt's roof poles meet the wall they push outward; a band of rope, woven cloth or wire cable at the top of the wall holds them in tension against this push.
The central compression ring plus the tension band lets a yurt roof span its room without internal posts, trusses or beams.

title: Adobe and Taos Pueblo
description: Adobe is unfired earth mixed with water and straw. The Tiwa-speaking people of Taos Pueblo have built and kept up multi-story adobe homes for centuries.

facts.text: The multi-storied adobe homes of the people of Taos Pueblo, in northern New Mexico, are estimated to have been built between 1000 and 1450 CE.
Tiwa is the native language of the people of Taos Pueblo, which became a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 1992.
At Taos Pueblo each home is owned by an individual family, which is responsible for maintaining it in the traditional way.
Taos Pueblo is made entirely of adobe: earth mixed with water and straw, then either poured into forms or made into sun-dried bricks.
Straw or grass in adobe bricks doesn't make them stronger, but it helps them shrink more evenly as they dry.
At Taos Pueblo, the roofs of each story are supported by large timbers called vigas, hauled down from the mountain forests.
Adobe bricks are not fired in a kiln, so they never permanently harden; they swell and shrink with their water content and grow weaker the wetter they get.
Adobe buildings deteriorate mainly because of moisture, so their survival depends on how well they shed water.
The outside surfaces of Taos Pueblo are continuously maintained by replastering them with thick layers of a mud and straw mixture.
Mud plaster bonds to adobe because the two are made of the same materials: clay, sand, water and straw or grass.

title: Thermal mass: walls that store heat
description: Heavy walls of earth and masonry store heat, so the inside warms hours after the outside and swings less, especially where days are hot and nights cool.

facts.text: Thermal mass is a material's ability to store heat; masonry materials tend to have high thermal mass.
In a house with high-thermal-mass walls, the inside temperature peaks a few hours after the outdoor peak, and the damping is greater where day-night temperature swings are larger.

title: Why stilt houses stand on stilts
description: Stilt houses such as South Sumatra's rumah panggung let floodwater pass beneath and let air under the floor to cut damp.

facts.text: Along the Musi River in South Sumatra, Indonesia, traditional stilt houses called rumah panggung stand about 1 to 2 m up, staying safe when floods reach an adult's knees or waist, as water flows beneath.
The open space beneath a rumah panggung lets in air and light, reducing the humidity that damages the wooden structure.

title: The prehistoric pile dwellings around the Alps
description: From about 5000 to 500 BC, farming communities around the Alps built wooden houses on piles in or near lakes, rivers and bogs.

facts.text: Around the Alps, from about 5000 to 500 BC, people built wooden houses on piles in or near water: on and in lakes, on river banks and in bogs.
Alpine lake dwellers burned their wooden piles to a point, drove them deep into the mud, packed heavy stones around them, and laid a platform of tree trunks and branches on top.
In the mid-19th century the Swiss archaeologist Ferdinand Keller argued the houses stood on platforms over the water; researchers now think they may have stood over swampy lake shore.
The wet ground preserved the pile dwellings' wood so well that 111 sites in six countries were inscribed as a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 2011.

title: The Roman domus and its atrium
description: A wealthy Roman's domus centered on the atrium, open to the sky through the compluvium, with the impluvium basin below; bigger houses added a peristyle.

facts.text: A Roman house's atrium was an open central court; rainwater came in through an opening in the roof, the compluvium, into a marble basin below, the impluvium.
In larger Roman houses, the family's private rooms clustered around a colonnaded court, the peristyle, beyond the atrium.

title: The Roman insula, an apartment block
description: In crowded Roman cities most people lived in insulae: brick-and-concrete apartment blocks of five or more stories with shops below and worse conditions higher up.

facts.text: In the great cities of the Roman Empire, crowding meant that by early imperial times the private house had given way to the insula, except for the very wealthy.
Insula is Latin for 'island'. Built of brick covered with concrete, insulae were often five or more stories high despite a limit of about 21 m (68 feet) under Augustus.
An insula's street level usually held workshops and shops; the homes above were reached by a shared staircase and got light and air from the street and an inner court.
Piped water reached only an insula's lower apartments, so people higher up used public facilities; cheap building made collapse and fire constant dangers.

title: Log building, from Colchis to New Sweden
description: Log houses stack whole trees crossed at the corners. Vitruvius described them among the Colchians; Scandinavian settlers brought the log cabin to America in 1638.

facts.text: Vitruvius described how the Colchians, with forests in plenty, laid whole trees flat and crossed them at the corners, building up walls to enclose a dwelling and filling gaps with chips and mud.
Colchis was an ancient region at the eastern end of the Black Sea, in the western part of modern Georgia.
Scandinavians introduced the log cabin to America when they settled New Sweden, around Delaware Bay, in 1638.
In its basic form a log cabin is four log walls joined at the corners into one room, or pen; Swedish builders filled the gaps with chinking of materials such as moss and clay.
The Nothnagle Log House in New Jersey, a one-room cabin built between 1638 and 1643 by Finnish settlers, is one of the oldest surviving wooden buildings in the United States.
English settlers in America preferred frame construction and did not adopt log building until the 18th century; Welsh and Scots-Irish settlers later carried log cabins to the western frontier.

title: Timber-framed houses and wattle and daub
description: In a timber-framed house the frame carries the load, and the panels between the timbers, often wattle and daub, only keep out the weather.

facts.text: In medieval timber-framed buildings, the timber frame is the load-bearing structure, and the open areas between the timbers are filled to keep the weather out.
Wattle and daub is a lattice of small woven timbers daubed with a mixture of mud, dung, water and straw.

title: Row houses and the Royal Crescent
description: Row houses share side walls in one continuous group; Bath's Royal Crescent put 30 of them behind one palace-like front.

facts.text: A row house is one of a series of houses connected by shared side walls, forming a continuous group.
Bath's Royal Crescent, designed by John Wood the Younger and begun in 1767, is a great curve of 30 attached townhouses behind one unified, palace-like front.
The Royal Crescent's unified, palace-like front was the first such design in English town architecture.
Each original Royal Crescent buyer bought a length of the front and had their own architect build the house behind it, so the backs don't match.

title: Why cities stack homes into apartments
description: Crowding and rising land values push cities to stack homes; in 19th-century Paris, apartments got smaller and cheaper the higher you climbed.

facts.text: Crowding and rising land values in cities made one-family homes less and less practical, so the multistory apartment house grew in importance.
In a typical 19th-century Parisian apartment building of four or five stories, the apartments, and the tenants' means, got smaller with each story up.

title: The Rietveld Schroder House's open plan
description: Truus Schroder and Gerrit Rietveld's 1924 house in Utrecht had an upper floor of sliding walls: one open space by day, three rooms at night, with a corner window that opens away.

facts.text: In 1924 Truus Schroder asked the Utrecht furniture designer Gerrit Rietveld to design her new home, and she played an important role in its design.
Both panes of the Rietveld Schroder House's upper-floor corner window swing open, dissolving the corner.
The Schroder house's upper floor was open space by day; in the evening the family used sliding walls to split it into three separate rooms.
The Rietveld Schroder House, designed in 1924 and lived in until 1985, became a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 2000.

title: The Eames House: a home from catalog parts
description: Charles and Ray Eames built their 1949 home from prefabricated catalog parts; its foundation and steel frame went up in 16 hours.

facts.text: Charles and Ray Eames's house, Case Study House #8 (1949), used prefabricated materials ordered from industrial and commercial catalogs.
Construction of the Eames House began in February 1949, and after 16 hours the foundation and steel frame were complete.
Charles and Ray Eames moved into the house on Christmas Eve 1949 and lived there for the rest of their lives.

title: Architecture Without Architects (MoMA, 1964)
description: Bernard Rudofsky's 1964 MoMA exhibition celebrated non-pedigreed architecture: old building traditions evolved and upheld by ordinary people.

facts.text: The architect and engineer Bernard Rudofsky directed 'Architecture Without Architects' at New York's Museum of Modern Art, opening in November 1964.
Rudofsky called his subject non-pedigreed architecture: old, sometimes ancient building traditions evolved and upheld by ordinary people.

title: Beam, arch and suspension bridges
description: A beam bridge bends; an arch bridge works in compression and needs strong foundations; a suspension deck hangs from curved cables in tension.

facts.text: A beam bridge carries loads by bending, with compression on top and tension below; an arch bridge carries loads mainly in compression and needs strong foundations.
In a suspension bridge the deck hangs from curved cables in tension, which carry the load to towers and to anchorages at each end.

title: Cable-stayed bridges
description: Nearly straight diagonal cables run from the deck directly to the towers; France's Millau Viaduct is one.

facts.text: In a cable-stayed bridge, nearly straight diagonal cables in tension carry the deck's weight directly to one or more towers.
France's Millau Viaduct, a cable-stayed bridge across the whole Tarn valley, opened in 2004; it was designed by architect Norman Foster with engineer Michel Virlogeux.

title: Cantilevers and the Forth Bridge
description: A cantilever is a beam supported at one end; the Forth Bridge (1890) joins three steel cantilevers with suspended spans.

facts.text: A cantilever is a beam supported at one end only, carrying load along its unsupported part.
Scotland's Forth Bridge, designed by John Fowler and Benjamin Baker and completed in 1890, joins three cantilevers with two suspended spans.
The Forth Bridge was the world's first major steel structure, and it became a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 2015.
In an 1887 demonstration, engineer Kaichi Watanabe sat suspended between Fowler and Baker, whose arms were in tension and sticks in compression.

title: The Brooklyn Bridge's caissons and caisson disease
description: Workers dug inside bottomless boxes kept dry by compressed air; coming up too fast caused the bends.

facts.text: The Brooklyn Bridge's towers stand on caissons: huge bottomless boxes sunk to the riverbed, where compressed air kept the water out while workers dug and the box sank, before being filled with concrete.
Caisson disease, the bends, struck workers when nitrogen bubbles formed in their blood as they came up from the caissons' pressurized air.

title: The Roeblings: the family who built the Brooklyn Bridge
description: John Roebling designed it and died in 1869; Washington directed it by telescope after the bends; Emily carried his instructions.

facts.text: John A. Roebling, the Brooklyn Bridge's designer, died of tetanus in 1869 after a ferry crushed his toes while he surveyed the tower sites.
His son Washington Roebling took over but was struck by caisson disease in 1872, and then directed the work through a telescope from his Brooklyn bedroom window.
Emily Warren Roebling carried her husband's directions to the engineers on the bridge.

title: The Brooklyn Bridge's steel cables and record span
description: Opened in 1883, it had the world's longest main span and was the first bridge to use steel cable wire.

facts.text: The Brooklyn Bridge opened on May 24, 1883; its 486-meter (1,595-foot) main span was the longest in the world when it opened.
The Brooklyn Bridge was the first bridge to use steel for its cable wire.
Emily Roebling rode in the first carriage across the finished bridge, carrying a rooster as a symbol of victory.

title: The 1887 protest against the Eiffel Tower
description: Leading artists called it useless and monstrous in Le Temps before it was built.

facts.text: On February 14, 1887, the newspaper Le Temps published an artists' protest against 'the useless and monstrous Eiffel Tower'; signers included architect Charles Garnier and composer Charles Gounod.

title: How the Eiffel Tower was designed and built
description: Engineers Koechlin and Nouguier conceived a 300 m iron pylon; Sauvestre dressed it; about 18,000 prefabricated pieces were riveted together.

facts.text: In 1884 Maurice Koechlin and Émile Nouguier, engineers in Gustave Eiffel's company, conceived a gigantic metal pylon 300 meters tall.
To make the tower more acceptable to the public, architect Stephen Sauvestre added large decorative arches between its feet, glass-walled rooms and stone pedestals.
The Eiffel Tower was built for Paris's 1889 International Exposition, which marked 100 years since the French Revolution.
Each of the Eiffel Tower's roughly 18,000 pieces was designed in advance, traced to a tenth of a millimeter, and pre-assembled into sections about 5 meters long.
The Eiffel Tower is built of wrought iron held together by some 2.5 million rivets, and it went up in about two years, from 1887 to 1889.

title: How radio saved the Eiffel Tower
description: Eiffel's 20-year permit was extended by 70 years because the tower proved useful for wireless telegraphy.

facts.text: Eiffel's permit for the tower ran for only 20 years, so its future after 1909 was uncertain.
In 1898 the first wireless telegraph trials linked the Eiffel Tower with the Panthéon.
The tower's value for radio won Eiffel a 70-year extension of his concession, starting in 1910.

title: Drill and blast: tunnelling through rock
description: Drill, load explosives, blast, ventilate, clear the muck, repeat; Mont Cenis pioneered air drills.

facts.text: In hard rock, tunnellers work in a cycle: drilling, loading explosives, blasting, clearing the fumes, and removing the broken rock, called muck.
The Mont Cenis Tunnel through the Alps (1857-71) pioneered rail-mounted drill carriages and compressed-air drills.

title: Immersed-tube tunnels
description: Prefabricated sections are floated out, sunk into a dredged trench and covered; Øresund is an example.

facts.text: In an immersed-tube tunnel, long prefabricated sections are floated to the site, sunk into a trench dredged in the bottom, and covered over.
The Detroit River Railroad Tunnel (1906-10) was the first immersed-tube tunnel, and since 1950 it has been the preferred way to tunnel under water.
The Øresund Tunnel between Denmark and Sweden is made of 20 elements, manufactured at a tunnel factory in Denmark; each weighs 55,000 tons.
A tunnel was chosen for that stretch of the Øresund link so it would not disrupt air traffic at Copenhagen Airport and large ships could pass.

title: A tunnel as an arch all the way round
description: Ground pushes on a tunnel from every side, so its shape is a continuous arch.

facts.text: A tunnel's basic shape is a continuous arch: because it must withstand pressure from all sides, the arch goes all the way around.

title: How dams hold back water
description: Water pressure grows with depth, so dams are thickest at the base; gravity dams use weight, arch dams push into the valley sides, embankment dams are mounds of earth or rock.

facts.text: Water pressure increases with depth (water squirts faster from a lower hole in a container), so a dam is built thickest at the bottom.

A gravity dam holds back water entirely by its own weight; an arch dam, built in a narrow gorge, passes the water's push into the valley sides; an embankment dam is a huge mound of earth or rock fill.
Embankment dams suit wide valleys and have become increasingly common.

title: Hoover Dam: an arch-gravity dam poured in columns
description: Its weight and arch action carry the water; it was built in columns cooled by pipes, since one pour would have taken 125 years to cool.
