facts.text: Engineers calculated that if Hoover Dam were poured in one go, its concrete would have taken 125 years to cool, and the stresses would have cracked it.
Hoover Dam is 660 feet thick at its base and 45 feet thick at its crest.
Hoover Dam, finished in 1936, is an arch-gravity dam: both its weight and its horizontal arch action carry the water load.
Hoover Dam was built as separate columns rising in five-foot lifts, cooled by 582 miles of embedded steel pipe carrying river water and then chilled water; cooling was done by March 1935.

title: Sea-level canals and lock canals
description: Suez is an open cut with no locks; at Panama, de Lesseps's sea-level plan failed and the US built locks up to Gatun Lake.

facts.text: Ferdinand de Lesseps, who had led the building of the Suez Canal (opened 1869), began a canal across Panama in 1881; his company failed in 1889.
The Suez Canal is an open cut without locks, linking the Mediterranean to the Red Sea and running through lakes such as Lake Timsah and the Bitter Lakes.
De Lesseps planned a sea-level canal at Panama, like Suez, and refused to adopt a plan with locks.
When the United States took over the Panama project in 1904, its engineers judged that digging all the way down to sea level would take too long and cost too much, so they built locks.
On the Panama Canal, a series of three locks lifts ships 85 feet (26 meters) to Gatun Lake, which was made by damming the Chagres River; the locks are filled by gravity, without pumps.

title: Beating disease at Panama
description: Mosquito-borne yellow fever and malaria crippled the French; Gorgas's mosquito control let the US finish in 1914.

facts.text: Yellow fever and malaria played a major role in depleting the French workforce at Panama.
William Gorgas, knowing that mosquitoes carried yellow fever and malaria, drained swamps and standing water, oiled water to kill larvae, and screened hospital wards.
The last Panama Canal worker to die of yellow fever caught it late in 1906.
The Panama Canal opened in August 1914.

title: The Eddystone lighthouses and Smeaton's tower
description: After two towers were lost, Smeaton's 1759 granite tower, shaped like an oak with dovetailed blocks, stood until its rock cracked.

facts.text: Henry Winstanley's Eddystone lighthouse of 1698, the first lighthouse built on a small rock in the open sea, was destroyed by a storm in 1703 that killed him.
The next Eddystone tower, John Rudyerd's, stood for 47 years until it burned in 1755.
John Smeaton's Eddystone lighthouse, finished in 1759, was built of Cornish granite and modeled on the shape of an oak tree for strength.
Smeaton locked the stones together with dovetailed joints and used a quick-setting cement that could withstand salty seawater.
Smeaton's tower was replaced in 1882 only because the rock beneath it cracked; its upper part was rebuilt on Plymouth Hoe.

title: The Fresnel lens
description: Fresnel's 1822 lens focused light that would scatter into one intense beam.

facts.text: In 1822 Augustin Fresnel completed a lighthouse lens design that focuses rays of light that would normally scatter into a single, intense beam.
Large first-order Fresnel lenses shine up to 21 miles out to sea.

title: How ships tell lighthouses apart
description: At night each light has its own flash pattern, its characteristic; by day, painted daymarks.

facts.text: Each lighthouse flashes its own pattern, called its characteristic, which mariners look up in light lists and charts to know which light they are seeing.
Today's Eddystone lighthouse shows two flashes every 10 seconds.
By day, lighthouses are identified by painted daymarks: Cape Hatteras has black and white spiral stripes, Bodie Island black and white bands, and Cape Lookout a checkerboard.

title: Shallow foundations and piles
description: Shallow foundations spread the load near the surface; piles carry it through weak soil to firmer ground.

facts.text: Shallow foundations sit near the surface and spread a building's load over the soil; where soil is weak, piles (long, slender columns) carry the load down through it to firmer soil or rock.

title: Why the Leaning Tower of Pisa leans
description: Begun in 1173 on a shallow footing in soft ground, it began to lean by 1178; a near-century pause let the ground firm up.

facts.text: Work on Pisa's bell tower began in 1173, and it began to lean when construction reached the second floor in 1178.
The tower stands on a footing only three meters deep, in soft ground that settled unevenly beneath it.
War between Italian city-states halted work for nearly a century, and the pause helped prevent an early collapse by letting the foundation stabilize.

When work resumed, engineer Giovanni di Simone made the new stories slightly taller on the short side to correct the tilt, but this backfired and the tower sank further; it was finished in the 14th century.

title: Straightening the Leaning Tower of Pisa
description: 1990-2001: soil removed from under the raised side pulled it back about 45 cm; stable by 2008.

facts.text: In 1990 the Leaning Tower of Pisa was closed to the public because its foundations were close to failing; it reopened in 2001.
Engineers including Imperial College's John Burland removed 38 cubic meters of soil from under the tower's raised side, straightening it by about 45 cm, to where it stood in 1838.
In 2008 engineers announced that the tower had stopped moving.

title: Why unreinforced brick buildings are dangerous in earthquakes
description: Brick with little or no steel collapses inward and outward, even in small quakes.

facts.text: FEMA's page on seismic building codes opens with the saying: 'earthquakes don't kill people, buildings do.'

Unreinforced masonry buildings have brick walls with little or no steel reinforcement; in earthquakes they often collapse both inward and outward, and even relatively small quakes can badly damage them.

title: Retrofitting brick buildings for earthquakes
description: Tying roof and walls together and bracing chimneys keeps old brick buildings intact so people can get out.

facts.text: Retrofits for brick buildings strengthen the roof-wall connection so walls and roof support each other, and brace chimneys; they help keep buildings intact so people can exit safely.

title: Base isolation
description: Rubber-and-steel isolators let the ground move beneath a building; Utah's Capitol has 265 of them.

facts.text: Between 2004 and 2008, the Utah State Capitol was fitted with 265 base isolators, made of alternating layers of rubber and steel around a lead core, between the building and the ground.

In an earthquake the isolators let the ground shift the Capitol up to two feet sideways while the building stays relatively still; the ground's movement heats the lead, which turns putty-like and soaks up energy.
The isolators cut the seismic impact on the Utah Capitol by roughly 75 to 80 percent.

title: Galloping Gertie: the Tacoma Narrows collapse
description: In 1940 wind twisted apart a narrow, girder-stiffened suspension bridge; it spurred aerodynamic research.

facts.text: The Tacoma Narrows Bridge in Washington State, nicknamed Galloping Gertie, opened on July 1, 1940, and collapsed on November 7, 1940, in a wind of about 42 mph.
No people died in the collapse, because the bridge had been closed to traffic in time.
Its narrow two-lane deck was stiffened by solid plate girders instead of open trusses, which did not absorb wind gusts, and it twisted in swings that grew steadily larger.
The collapse spurred research into how wind acts on bridges; the replacement, opened in 1950, used a web truss, and later suspension bridges were designed with its lessons.

title: Chicago after the 1871 fire
description: The 1871 fire cleared central Chicago and set off a land rush; the first skyscrapers, with steel frames, elevators and new foundations, followed 10 to 15 years later.

facts.text: The Great Chicago Fire began on October 8, 1871; about 300 people died and roughly one in three Chicagoans was left homeless.

Right after the 1871 fire, Chicago's new buildings looked much like the old ones and a land rush began within months; the earliest skyscrapers, 8 to 10 stories with steel frames, elevators and innovative foundations, came 10 to 15 years later.

title: The Chicago school
description: Jenney, Burnham, Root, Adler and Sullivan developed the skyscraper in late 19th-century Chicago, starting with frame buildings like the Home Insurance Building.

facts.text: The Chicago school (Jenney, Burnham, Root, Adler, Sullivan and others) developed the skyscraper in the late 19th century; Jenney designed the Home Insurance Building, and Chicago has been called the birthplace of modern architecture.

title: Sullivan: form follows function
description: Sullivan's 1896 essay: a tall building's outside should show its uses, from shops at the base to identical office floors to a closing attic; the Wainwright Building reads like a column.

facts.text: In his 1896 essay 'The Tall Office Building Artistically Considered', Louis Sullivan wrote that 'form ever follows function': a grand, open street floor, identical office tiers made to look alike 'because they are all alike', and an attic that shows the offices have ended.

Critics compared a tall building to a classical column (base, shaft, capital); Adler and Sullivan's 10-story Wainwright Building in St. Louis (1890-91) has a two-story stone base, seven stories of continuous brick piers, and a leafy frieze under an overhanging roof.
Sullivan stressed a tall building's vertical elements and minimized its horizontals, to make it a 'proud and soaring' unity.

title: The safety elevator
description: Otis's 1854 brake gripped the guide rails if the rope failed; the 1857 passenger elevator made buildings over four or five stories practical.

facts.text: In 1854, at New York's Crystal Palace, Elisha Otis rode his raised elevator platform and had its rope cut; his safety device held it.
Otis's safety device gripped the guide rails when the hoist rope lost its tension, so a broken rope set the brake itself.
The first safe passenger elevator, installed in 1857 in the E.V. Haughwout store in New York City, made buildings of more than four or five stories practical.

title: From attic to penthouse
description: Elevators made upper floors as easy to reach as lower ones, turning the poor's attic into the prized penthouse and helping shape modern cities.

facts.text: New York's Equitable Life Assurance Building (1870), said to be the city's first office building with a passenger elevator, made its upper floors as convenient as the lower ones, and even more desirable.
Before elevators, the attic was the hard-to-reach retreat of the poor; thanks to the elevator it became the sought-after penthouse, and by the 1920s the top floor was in its heyday.
By opening the way to higher buildings, the elevator played a decisive role in creating the urban geography of many modern cities.

title: The Empire State Building's record build
description: The 102-story Empire State Building went up in about 410 days (1930-31), its frame rising about four and a half stories a week.

facts.text: The 102-story Empire State Building was built in about 410 days, from March 17, 1930, to its opening on May 1, 1931, when President Herbert Hoover pressed a button in Washington, D.C.
The Empire State Building's framework rose at about four and a half stories per week; its architects were Shreve, Lamb & Harmon and its builders Starrett Bros. & Eken.

title: How the Empire State Building was built so fast
description: Overlapping design and construction, digging while demolishing, just-in-time deliveries and a site railway.

facts.text: Empire State Building construction began before the design was complete, foundations were dug while the old Waldorf-Astoria hotel on the site was still being demolished, deliveries arrived just in time, and railway tracks moved materials on site.

title: The Empire State Building's design
description: Art Deco, 1,250 feet with a spire meant for airships, and the world's tallest building until 1971.

facts.text: Designed in Art Deco style, the Empire State Building rose 1,250 feet (381 meters) with its spire, which was first meant as a mooring station for airships; it was the world's tallest building until 1971.

title: Wind vortices and resonance
description: Vortices shed alternately from a tower's sides push it across the wind; timed to its natural frequency, like pushes on a swing, they make it sway harder.

facts.text: As wind flows past a tall building, vortices form and shed alternately from each side, pushing and pulling the building across the wind direction.
Like pushes on a swing timed to its natural rhythm, vortices shedding at a building's natural frequency make it sway harder; at a minimum, upper floors become uncomfortable.

title: Taming the wind: shape and dampers
description: Changing shape with height confuses the wind; softened corners, openings, wind tunnels and dampers like Taipei 101's steel sphere help too.

facts.text: Varying a tower's cross section with height 'confuses' the wind so vortices lose coherence; softened corners, openings for the wind, wind-tunnel tests and dampers also tame sway.
Taipei 101 has a steel sphere weighing 660 metric tons suspended between its 87th and 92nd floors, in the middle of the building, to keep it steady in strong winds.

title: Burj Khalifa: the tallest building
description: As of 2026 the CTBUH ranks Burj Khalifa (2010, 828 m), designed by SOM's Adrian Smith and William F. Baker, as the world's tallest.

facts.text: As of 2026, the Council on Tall Buildings and Urban Habitat (CTBUH) ranks Dubai's Burj Khalifa, completed in 2010, as the world's tallest building at 828 meters.
Burj Khalifa was designed by Skidmore, Owings & Merrill (SOM), with Adrian Smith as architect and William F. Baker as structural engineer, and formally opened on January 4, 2010.

title: Burj Khalifa's Y plan and buttressed core
description: A Y-shaped plan from a desert flower, with three wings bracing a six-sided core, and wings that step back in a spiral to confuse the wind.

facts.text: Burj Khalifa's Y-shaped plan abstracts the local Hymenocallis desert flower and draws on patterns of Islamic architecture; it maximizes views toward the Arabian Gulf and reduces wind forces.
In Burj Khalifa's buttressed core, a six-sided central concrete core is braced by three wings, each with its own concrete core and perimeter columns.
Burj Khalifa's wings step back in a spiral as it rises, so the wind meets a different shape at each tier and its vortices never coalesce: 'confusing the wind', a strategy backed by wind-tunnel tests.

title: The curtain wall
description: A nonbearing outer wall of glass, metal or masonry hung on the structural frame.

facts.text: A curtain wall is a nonbearing wall of glass, metal or masonry attached to a building's exterior structural frame.

title: The rise of the glass tower
description: Air conditioning and cheap postwar energy made all-glass towers practical; Lever House (1952) led the way in New York.

facts.text: Fully glazed towers became practical in the mid-20th century with better air conditioning and cheap, abundant energy; after World War II, low energy costs boosted the idea of the tower as a glass prism.
Lever House (1952), designed by Gordon Bunshaft of SOM, was the first commercial building in New York City with a glass curtain wall; extruded aluminum held its glass, and it was widely copied.

title: Glass and the sun
description: Glass buildings struggle with solar heat, from the Crystal Palace to the Walkie-Talkie's focused glare.

facts.text: Records from the Crystal Palace (1851) show its indoor temperatures were extremely unstable; the glass building amplified peak summer heat.

In 2013, sunlight reflected and concentrated by the concave glass face of London's 20 Fenchurch Street, the 'Walkie-Talkie', melted part of a parked Jaguar; a permanent sunshade of horizontal aluminum fins was later approved.

title: Building a skyscraper, step by step
description: Dig a pit, sink piles to bedrock, raise the steel frame by crane, pour floors on steel decking, bolt on the outer wall and fit out, with phases overlapping.

facts.text: Skyscraper construction usually begins with digging a pit for the foundation; piles are sunk through the soil until they are embedded in the bedrock.
Cranes lift each steel beam into place to be bolted or welded; floors are made of corrugated steel decking with about 5 to 10 cm (2 to 4 inches) of concrete poured on top.
Panels of glass, metal or stone are bolted to a skyscraper's frame as its outer wall, wiring, pipes and elevators are installed, and work on several phases goes on at the same time.

title: Core-first construction
description: A concrete core with stairs, elevators and risers is cast in a self-climbing form, and the steel frame follows it up.

facts.text: In core-first construction, a concrete core holding stairways, elevators and utility risers is cast in a self-climbing form, a giant mold, and the steel framing follows once the forms have climbed clear.

title: Lunch atop a Skyscraper
description: The staged 1932 photo of real ironworkers eating lunch on a beam 850 feet up the RCA Building.

facts.text: On September 20, 1932, 11 ironworkers ate lunch on a steel beam 850 feet up the RCA Building at Rockefeller Center; they were real ironworkers posing for a photographer promoting the project.

title: Falls and fall protection
description: Falls are the leading cause of construction deaths; US rules require fall protection from six feet: guardrails, harnesses and nets.

facts.text: Falls are the leading cause of death in US construction: in 2024 there were 389 fatal falls to a lower level out of 1,034 construction fatalities, more than a third.
US rules require fall protection in construction at six feet; it includes guardrails and toe-boards around open edges, safety harnesses and lines, and safety nets.

title: The hard hat
description: Bullard's steamed-canvas Hard Boiled Hat, modeled on WWI helmets for miners, spread to construction; Hoover Dam first required it.

facts.text: After World War I, Edward W. Bullard made a safety helmet of steamed canvas and glue, the Hard Boiled Hat, inspired by army 'doughboy' helmets and meant for miners; Hoover Dam was the first project where employers required hard hats.

title: The Chrysler Building's secret spire
description: In 1929 Van Alen hoisted a secretly assembled spire in about 90 minutes to beat 40 Wall Street; the Chrysler held the title until 1931.

facts.text: Racing 40 Wall Street, William Van Alen had the Chrysler Building's spire assembled secretly inside its crown in five sections and hoisted into place in about 90 minutes on October 23, 1929.
Built between 1928 and 1930, the Chrysler Building rose to 1,046 feet and held the tallest-building record until the Empire State Building opened in 1931.

title: What counts as the top
description: The CTBUH measures to the architectural top: spires count, antennas don't, which is how the Petronas Towers outranked the Sears Tower in 1998.

facts.text: In 1998 the Petronas Twin Towers in Kuala Lumpur, 452 meters with their spires, became the world's tallest, though Chicago's Sears Tower roof was more than 200 feet higher: the spires counted as architecture.
The CTBUH ranks buildings by height to their architectural top: spires count, antennas don't.

title: The race to the top: a timeline
description: The tallest-building title passed from New York to Chicago, Kuala Lumpur, Taipei and Dubai.

facts.text: New York's World Trade Center towers opened in April 1973, and Chicago's Sears Tower, completed in May 1973, surpassed them as the world's tallest building.
Taipei 101, 508 meters tall including its spire, was completed in 2004 and took the tallest-building title from the Petronas Towers.

title: Where the word skyscraper comes from
description: A sailors' word for a mast-top sail (1794) became the name for very tall buildings in 1888 Chicago.

facts.text: 'Skyscraper' meant a light sail at the top of a mast (1794), and earlier a racehorse, before it meant a very tall city building, first recorded in 1888 in a Chicago context; German has Wolkenkratzer ('cloud scraper') and French gratte-ciel ('scrape-sky').

title: New York's 1916 zoning and the wedding-cake tower
description: After the Equitable Building's seven-acre shadow, the 1916 Zoning Resolution shaped slender towers and tiered wedding-cake buildings.

facts.text: In 1915 New York's Equitable Building rose without setbacks to 538 feet and cast a seven-acre shadow over neighboring buildings, setting the stage for reform.
New York's 1916 Zoning Resolution, the nation's first comprehensive zoning ordinance, controlled the size and shape of buildings and fostered slender towers and tiered 'wedding cake' buildings.

title: Gaudí's Barcelona: the Sagrada Família and trencadís
description: Gaudí took over the Sagrada Família in 1883 and worked on it until his death in 1926; his broken-tile trencadís mosaics cover curves such as Park Güell's bench.

facts.text: Gaudí was commissioned to build Barcelona's Sagrada Família in 1883, a year after its first cornerstone was laid.
The Sagrada Família occupied Gaudí until he died in 1926; only one transept, with one of its towers, was finished then.
The Sagrada Família's central Tower of Jesus Christ was completed in February 2026; finishing work continues.
Trencadís is a mosaic of broken ceramic tile pieces; Gaudí used it because small pieces can cover curved surfaces.
Park Güell's long, undulating bench is covered in brightly colored trencadís.
UNESCO lists seven of Gaudí's works in and near Barcelona as World Heritage, first inscribed in 1984 and extended in 2005.

title: Gaudí's upside-down hanging models
description: Gaudí hung weighted cords to find shapes in pure tension, then turned them upside down to get arches and columns in pure compression.

facts.text: Gaudí designed with hanging models: cords loaded with small bags of weight. Upside down, their shapes gave arches in compression.
Gaudí worked out the hanging-model method for the church at the Colònia Güell, near Barcelona, and carried it into the Sagrada Família.

title: Standing like a tree: Gaudí's tilted columns
description: Gaudí's structures stand without external buttresses, on piers and columns that tilt to carry diagonal thrusts, branching like a forest in the Sagrada Família.

facts.text: Gaudí meant his buildings to stand without external buttresses, as a tree stands, on piers and columns tilted to carry diagonal thrusts.
For the Sagrada Família, Gaudí designed a symbolic forest of twisting piers.

title: Fallingwater and organic architecture
description: Wright set Fallingwater (1935-37) over the falls of Bear Run as stacked concrete trays anchored to a stone chimney, an example of his organic architecture.

facts.text: The Kaufmanns expected a house facing the falls of Bear Run; Wright instead cantilevered Fallingwater directly over them.
Frank Lloyd Wright designed Fallingwater in 1935 as a weekend retreat for the Kaufmann family; it was finished in 1937.
Wright called his approach organic architecture: buildings in harmony with their site, joining people and nature.
Echoing nearby rock ledges, Fallingwater is a stack of concrete trays anchored to a central chimney of local sandstone.

title: How a cantilever works
description: A cantilever is a beam supported at one end; unlike a simple beam, its upper half is stretched and its lower half squeezed.

facts.text: A cantilever is a beam supported at only one end, with the other end free.
In a loaded cantilever, the upper half of the beam is stretched in tension and the lower half is squeezed in compression.
Fallingwater's concrete terraces carry steel reinforcing rods inside.

title: Fallingwater's sagging cantilevers and their repair
description: Fallingwater's terraces sagged for decades; in 2001-2002 tightened high-strength steel cables stopped them.

facts.text: By 1955 the Kaufmanns had measured Fallingwater's terraces tilting down about four inches.
In 2001-2002, engineers anchored high-strength steel cables beneath Fallingwater and tightened them along its beams, stopping the sag.

title: A house as a machine for living in
description: Le Corbusier's 1923 line 'a house is a machine for living in' meant a house should serve the body efficiently; the Villa Savoye even curves to fit the car.

facts.text: In his 1923 book Vers une architecture, Le Corbusier wrote: 'La maison est une machine à habiter', a house is a machine for living in.
Le Corbusier said a house is first a machine for living, serving the body's need for comfort, and then a place for meditation and beauty.
The Villa Savoye's ground floor curves to fit the turning radius of the family car, which drove in under the pilotis.

title: The Dom-ino frame
description: Le Corbusier's 1914 Dom-ino system (three slabs, six posts, a staircase) did away with load-bearing walls, freeing plans and facades.

facts.text: Le Corbusier's Dom-ino system of 1914 is three concrete floor slabs, six posts and a staircase: a module that can be repeated.
Because the Dom-ino's posts carry the floors, it needs no load-bearing walls, freeing the layout and facades for long strip windows.

title: Le Corbusier's five points and the Villa Savoye
description: Pilotis, roof garden, free plan, long horizontal windows and free facade (theorized 1927), best shown in the Villa Savoye (1928-31).

facts.text: Le Corbusier's five points for a new architecture (1927): pilotis, a roof garden, a free plan, long horizontal windows and a free facade.
The Villa Savoye at Poissy, France, built 1928-1931, is the house that best illustrates the five points.
In 2016, UNESCO listed seventeen of Le Corbusier's works, in seven countries, as World Heritage.

title: The Bauhaus school
description: Founded by Gropius in Weimar in 1919, the Bauhaus taught art and craft equally in two-teacher workshops, aimed design at mass manufacture, and was closed in 1933.

facts.text: Walter Gropius founded the Bauhaus in Weimar, Germany, in 1919 by combining an academy of arts with a school of arts and crafts.
The Bauhaus trained students equally in art and in expert craftsmanship, to end the split between the two.
Each Bauhaus workshop had two teachers: an artist called the Form Master, who taught theory, and a craftsman, who taught technique.
Gropius steered Bauhaus design toward mass manufacture rather than one-off handicraft.
The Bauhaus moved from Weimar to Dessau in 1925 and to Berlin in 1932; the Nazi regime forced it to close in 1933.

title: Breuer's tubular steel chair
description: Marcel Breuer's 1925 tubular steel club chair, inspired by bicycle handlebars, suited industrial production.

facts.text: Marcel Breuer's tubular steel club chair of 1925 was inspired by the handlebars of his bicycle.
Breuer made it the year he became master of the Bauhaus cabinet-making workshop; he saw tubular steel as suited to industrial production.
Breuer's club chair is often called the Wassily chair.

title: The Bauhaus building in Dessau
description: Gropius's Dessau building (opened 1926) wraps its workshop wing in steel and glass, and the school's own workshops made its lamps and furniture.

facts.text: Gropius's office designed the school's new building in Dessau, which opened on 4 December 1926.
The Dessau workshop wing's steel and glass facade is drawn around it like a curtain, so the workshops are visible from outside.
The Dessau building's lamps and tubular steel furniture came from the school's own workshops; Gropius designed the door handles.

title: Mies van der Rohe: less is more
description: Mies's motto 'less is more' and his 'skin and bones' architecture of exposed structure; he directed the Bauhaus from 1930 to 1933.

facts.text: Mies van der Rohe's motto was 'less is more', summing up his approach of elegant simplicity.
Mies directed the Bauhaus from 1930 until the Nazi regime forced it to close in 1933.

title: The Barcelona Pavilion
description: Mies and Lilly Reich's 1929 German Pavilion: slender steel columns carry the roof, so walls of glass and stone stand freely; dismantled 1930, rebuilt 1983-86.

facts.text: Mies van der Rohe and Lilly Reich designed Germany's pavilion for the 1929 Barcelona International Exposition.
The Barcelona Pavilion was taken apart in 1930 and rebuilt on its original site from 1983 to 1986.
In the Barcelona Pavilion, eight slender chrome-clad steel columns hold up the flat roof, so walls can stand freely as screens.
The pavilion's walls are glass, travertine, green marble and golden onyx.

title: The Farnsworth House
description: Mies's glass box (designed 1945, built 1950-51) on the Fox River floodplain, raised above the highest flood then known, has since flooded badly.

facts.text: Mies's Farnsworth House (designed 1945, built 1950-51) is a glass box raised on steel on the Fox River floodplain near Chicago.
Mies set the Farnsworth House one foot above the highest flood recorded at the time.
In the 1996 flood, water stood more than five feet deep inside the Farnsworth House.

title: The Sydney Opera House's spherical solution
description: Utzon found that every shell could be cut from one sphere, so the roof could be made of standard precast parts; the orange eureka story is a myth.

facts.text: In 1957, Danish architect Jørn Utzon won the international competition for a Sydney opera house, against 233 entries.
From 1958 to 1962, Utzon and engineers at Arup tried parabolic, then ellipsoid, then spherical geometry to make the shells buildable.
By late 1961, Utzon saw that every shell could be derived from the surface of a single sphere.
With one shared geometry, the shells could be split into standard parts, prefabricated and assembled on site.
The Sydney Opera House calls the story of Utzon's eureka moment peeling an orange a popular myth.

title: Utzon's resignation and the Opera House's completion
description: Utzon resigned in 1966 after a dispute with the New South Wales government and never returned; Peter Hall's team completed the building in 1973.

facts.text: In February 1966, after a dispute with the New South Wales government, Utzon resigned; a team led by Peter Hall took over the design.
Utzon left Australia in April 1966 and never returned to see the Opera House completed.
The Sydney Opera House was completed in 1973.
The Sydney Opera House was added to UNESCO's World Heritage List in 2007.

title: Zaha Hadid, from paper architect to Pritzker
description: Hadid, born in Baghdad, explored designs through painting; long called a 'paper architect', she became the first woman to win the Pritzker Prize in 2004.

facts.text: For years Zaha Hadid was labeled a 'paper architect', because her designs, often competition winners, went unbuilt.
In 1983 Hadid won an international competition for The Peak, a leisure club in Hong Kong.
Hadid was born in Baghdad in 1950, studied mathematics in Beirut, then trained as an architect in London.
Painting and drawing, especially early on, were Hadid's ways of investigating a design.
Hadid's work drew on Kazimir Malevich and the Suprematists, with a sense of fragmentation, instability and movement.
In 2004 Zaha Hadid became the first woman to win the Pritzker Architecture Prize.

title: The Vitra Fire Station: movement frozen
description: Hadid's first major built work (1993) is a layered series of sharply angled concrete planes, described by her office as 'movement frozen'.

facts.text: Hadid's first major built work was the Vitra Fire Station in Weil am Rhein, Germany, finished in 1993.
The Vitra Fire Station is a series of sharply angled, tilted planes of exposed concrete.
Zaha Hadid Architects called the fire station 'movement frozen', tense and alert, ready to explode into action.
The Vitra Fire Station no longer houses fire engines; it is now used for exhibitions and events.

title: Hadid's flowing later buildings
description: Later Hadid buildings flow: the Heydar Aliyev Center (2012) seems to lift and fold out of its plaza, blurring floor, wall and roof.

facts.text: Zaha Hadid Architects' Heydar Aliyev Center in Baku, completed in 2012, seems to lift, curve and fold out of its plaza.
In the Heydar Aliyev Center, the boundaries between floor, wall, ceiling and roof are blurred into one surface.

title: Brutalism's name: béton brut
description: Brutalism's name probably comes from béton brut, French for raw concrete; Le Corbusier's later concrete kept the marks of its formwork.

facts.text: Brutalism's name probably comes from béton brut (raw concrete), Le Corbusier's phrase while building his Unité d'Habitation in 1952.
From the 1950s, Le Corbusier left materials unfinished, including concrete bearing the marks of its formwork.

title: The New Brutalism: honest materials
description: Reyner Banham named 'The New Brutalism' in 1955, holding up the Smithsons' Hunstanton school as made of what it appears to be made of.

facts.text: In a 1955 essay, the critic Reyner Banham named a trend in British architecture 'The New Brutalism'.
Banham held up Alison and Peter Smithson's school at Hunstanton as a building 'made of what it appears to be made of'.
Brutalism was not only concrete: the Smithsons wanted every material, brick, timber or glass, honestly expressed.

title: Why people argue about Brutalism
description: Brutalism is loved and loathed: fans see post-war ambition, critics a dystopian landscape-destroyer, as Portsmouth's Tricorn Centre showed.

facts.text: Portsmouth's Brutalist Tricorn Centre opened in 1966; the critic Ian Nairn wrote, 'At last there is something to shout about in Portsmouth.'
Prince Charles called the Tricorn Centre 'a mildewed lump of elephant droppings'; writer Jonathan Meades compared it to Stonehenge.
The Tricorn Centre was demolished in 2004.
Historic England calls Brutalism loved and loathed, one of the most controversial architectural styles of the 20th century.
To fans, Brutalism shows the post-war drive to rebuild towns to serve people; to critics, it was a dystopian landscape-destroyer.

title: Designing the Guggenheim Bilbao
description: Gehry's museum (1997) used CATIA aerospace software to turn complex curves into structure, and is skinned in about 33,000 thin titanium sheets.

facts.text: Bilbao grew on iron, steel and shipbuilding, and went through a severe economic crisis in the 1970s and 1980s.
Frank Gehry's Guggenheim Museum Bilbao opened in 1997, a joint venture of the Guggenheim Foundation and the Basque regional government.
For Gehry's mathematically complex design, his team used CATIA, software first built for the aerospace industry, to design and build it.
Gehry chose titanium after watching a sample pinned outside his office; about 33,000 thin sheets change color with weather and light.

title: The Bilbao effect, and its skeptics
description: About 20 million visitors in 20 years gave rise to the 'Bilbao effect'; Witold Rybczynski argued eye-catching museums don't reliably repeat it.

facts.text: The Guggenheim Bilbao drew about 20 million visitors in its first 20 years.
The 'Bilbao effect' names the idea that one iconic building can transform a city's fortunes, as Bilbao became a major tourist destination.
In 2011, critic Witold Rybczynski argued that eye-catching museum architecture doesn't by itself bring crowds, citing Seattle and Denver.

title: The Pritzker Architecture Prize
description: Founded in 1979 by the Pritzker family, the prize honors a living architect's built work each year; Gehry (1989), Utzon (2003) and Hadid (2004) won it.

facts.text: The Pritzker Architecture Prize was established in 1979 by the Pritzker family of Chicago, through their Hyatt Foundation.
Each year the Pritzker Prize honors a living architect whose built work shows talent, vision and commitment.
The Pritzker Prize is often called architecture's Nobel, and many of its procedures are modeled on the Nobel Prize.
A Pritzker laureate receives $100,000 and a bronze medallion.
Frank Gehry won the Pritzker Prize in 1989 and Jørn Utzon in 2003.

title: What makes a city
description: Childe's checklist for the earliest cities: size, big public works, writing and full-time specialists.

facts.text: The archaeologist V. Gordon Childe listed 10 signs of the earliest cities, including larger settlements, large-scale public works, writing and full-time specialists.

title: Uruk, an early city
description: Uruk in southern Mesopotamia: the largest settlement of its time, with mosaic-clad mud-brick buildings, a wall and the first ledgers.

facts.text: By around 3200 BCE, Uruk was the largest settlement in southern Mesopotamia, if not the world, a city of monumental mud-brick buildings.
Uruk lies in what is now southeastern Iraq, northwest of Ur.
Uruk's monumental mud-brick buildings were decorated with mosaics of painted clay cones pressed into their walls.
Uruk was enclosed by brick walls about 10 km around, which legend says were built by the hero Gilgamesh.
The earliest written records in Sumerian are picture-sign tablets from Uruk, from about the end of the 4th millennium BCE: lists or ledgers of goods, with numerals and names.

title: Grid street plans
description: Grids are ancient (Mohenjo-daro), named for Hippodamus, used by Roman towns and spread across America because they divide land simply.

facts.text: Mohenjo-daro, the largest city of the Indus civilization (about 2600 to 1900 BCE), was laid out with remarkable regularity in about a dozen blocks.
Hippodamus of Miletus, a 5th-century BCE Greek planner who laid out Athens's port of Piraeus, gave his name to grid plans, though he did not invent them.
Many Roman towns were laid out on a grid, with two main streets crossing at right angles.
William Penn's 1682 grid for Philadelphia traveled west with American pioneers because it was the simplest way to divide surveyed land.

title: Manhattan's 1811 grid
description: New York's commissioners gridded Manhattan to 155th Street because right-angled houses are cheapest to build.

facts.text: New York's Commissioners' Plan of 1811 laid a grid of streets and avenues over Manhattan, from today's Houston Street up to 155th Street.
The 1811 commissioners wrote that straight-sided, right-angled houses 'are the most cheap to build, and the most convenient to live in.'

title: Why towns built walls
description: Walls meant security, paid for by taxes like murage; gates funnelled carts and walkers through arches.

facts.text: Fears of invasion, uprising and civil war made medieval town walls seem a necessary security.
English towns could get royal permission to collect a tax called murage to pay for work on their walls.
A medieval town's main gate could have several archways: a large one for wheeled traffic and one or two smaller ones for people on foot.

title: From walls to boulevards
description: Walls cramped growing cities, so many came down; boulevards and Vienna's Ringstrasse took their place.

facts.text: Boulevard comes from French for the top surface of a rampart, a garbled borrowing of Middle Dutch bolwerc, the same word that gave English bulwark.
As cities grew, their walls caused overcrowding, blocked out air and light, and led to very poor sanitation.
By the 18th century, town walls and gates seemed a hindrance to growth and traffic, and gates were often removed as too narrow.
In the late 17th century, Louis XIV had an old Paris city wall razed and replaced with a wide tree-lined promenade: a boulevard.
On 20 December 1857, Emperor Franz Joseph ordered Vienna's city walls torn down for the Ringstrasse, a grand boulevard whose first section opened in 1865.

title: The first public parks
description: Paxton's Birkenhead Park (1847), paid for by the houses around it, inspired Olmsted's 'People's Garden' ideal.

facts.text: Birkenhead Park, opened in 1847 and designed by Joseph Paxton, was the first public park in the UK created at public expense.
Birkenhead Park was paid for from the profit on house plots sold around its edge.
After visiting Birkenhead Park in 1850, Frederick Law Olmsted wrote that democratic America had nothing comparable with this 'People's Garden'.

title: Central Park by design
description: Olmsted and Vaux's Greensward plan: a hand-built landscape for a crowded city, with crosstown roads sunk out of sight.

facts.text: Central Park was planned as New York's population boomed and many immigrants lived in crowded, unhealthy conditions.
In 1858, Olmsted and the architect Calvert Vaux won the design competition for Central Park with their Greensward plan.
The Greensward plan hid Central Park's crosstown roads below the landscape, out of sight of park visitors.
Central Park's landscapes are man-made, built by hand; workers planted 500,000 trees, shrubs and vines.

title: Public squares
description: Siena's Campo: a shell-shaped meeting place whose nine paving sections point to the town hall.

facts.text: Siena's Piazza del Campo is shell-shaped, its brick paving divided into nine parts that point toward the Palazzo Pubblico, the seat of government.
The nine parts of the Campo recall the Government of the Nine, which ruled Siena from 1287 to 1355.
The Campo was made as a meeting place for citizens, with markets, games and political events; the Palio horse race is held there twice a year.

title: What makes streets and plazas work
description: Whyte's sitting space, Jacobs's eyes upon the street, and Copenhagen's car-free Strøget.

facts.text: Filming New York plazas with time-lapse cameras, William H. Whyte found that 'people tend to sit where there are places to sit' (1980): sitting space mattered more than open space.
In The Death and Life of Great American Cities (1961), Jane Jacobs argued that a well-used street is apt to be safe, watched by 'eyes upon the street' from buildings facing it.
In 1962, Copenhagen made its main street, Strøget, car-free as an experiment, despite warnings that no cars would mean no customers.
According to the Global Designing Cities Initiative, Strøget succeeded and increased revenue for local shops.

title: The first subways
description: London's Metropolitan Railway (1863) ran steam trains in cut-and-cover trenches; electric deep tubes followed in 1890.

facts.text: The world's first underground railway, London's Metropolitan Railway, opened on 10 January 1863 with steam locomotives.
The Metropolitan was built by cut and cover: trenches dug along the streets, given brick sides and roofed with girders or a brick arch.
In 1890 London opened the first electric underground railway, the first deep 'tube', dug by tunnelling instead of trenching.

title: Metro-land: railways build suburbs
description: The Metropolitan Railway marketed 'Metro-land' and built housing on its own land to create commuters.

facts.text: In 1915 the Metropolitan Railway began selling the countryside along its line as 'Metro-land', a place for commuters to live.
From 1919, a company set up by the Metropolitan Railway built housing estates on spare land the railway owned along its line.

title: Transport, cars and suburbs
description: Suburbs follow transport: ferries, trolleys, then cars and the 1956 interstate highways; Levittown became the symbol.

facts.text: Levittown, New York, built by Levitt and Sons from 1946 to 1951, was an early completely preplanned, mass-produced housing development of more than 17,000 homes.
Levittown became a national symbol of suburbia during the building boom after World War II.
Early American suburbs grew along transport: Brooklyn Heights after an 1814 ferry to Manhattan, and later trolley-car suburbs.
After World War II, federal policy and highway construction sped up the growth of American suburbs.
The Federal-Aid Highway Act, signed on 29 June 1956, authorized 41,000 miles of interstate highways, with the federal government paying 90 percent.

title: The sprawl debate
description: UN-Habitat sees car-driven sprawl as wasteful of land; historian Robert Bruegmann argues it brings mobility, privacy and choice.

facts.text: UN-Habitat says urban sprawl is largely driven by the automobile, poor planning and land speculation, and uses land less efficiently.
Historian Robert Bruegmann argued in 2005 that sprawl is as old as cities and has given millions mobility, privacy and choice once reserved for the rich.

title: Informal settlements
description: UN-Habitat: over 1.1 billion people in slums or informal settlements, defined by five household deprivations and insecure tenure.

facts.text: According to UN-Habitat, more than 1.1 billion people live in slums or informal settlements.
UN-Habitat counts a household as a slum household if it lacks one or more of: durable housing, enough living space, improved water, improved sanitation or secure tenure.
UN-Habitat describes informal settlements as areas where residents lack secure tenure, basic services are often missing, and homes may not meet planning and building rules.

title: Public housing: Karl-Marx-Hof
description: Red Vienna's kilometer-long Karl-Marx-Hof built on only about 18% of its site, around courtyards and shared facilities.

facts.text: Vienna's Karl-Marx-Hof, designed by Karl Ehn in the Red Vienna social housing era (1919 to 1934), is about 1,100 meters long and originally held 1,382 apartments.
Only about 18% of the Karl-Marx-Hof's site was built on; the rest is courtyards and green space, alongside laundries, baths and kindergartens.

title: Incremental housing
description: Aravena's 'half of a good house': build the hard half on well-located land and let families finish the rest.

facts.text: Alejandro Aravena's firm ELEMENTAL designs social housing it calls 'half of a good house', leaving room for residents to finish their homes themselves.
According to the Pritzker Prize, this 'incremental housing' lets social housing be built on more expensive land, closer to jobs and opportunity.
Alejandro Aravena of Chile won the 2016 Pritzker Architecture Prize.

title: L'Enfant's Washington
description: A capital chosen by law and drawn in 1791: diagonal avenues over a grid, the Capitol on its 'pedestal'.

facts.text: The Residence Act of 1790 let President George Washington choose the site of a brand-new national capital.
Pierre L'Enfant's 1791 plan for Washington laid diagonal avenues radiating from the Capitol across a grid of streets, with circles, squares and parks where avenues meet.
L'Enfant put the Capitol on Jenkins' Hill, a site he called 'a pedestal waiting for a monument'.
L'Enfant refused to produce drawings for the Capitol, saying he carried the design 'in his head', and was dismissed in 1792.

title: Brasília
description: A capital built in the interior, opened in 1960: Costa's airplane-shaped plan and Niemeyer's buildings, praised and criticized.

facts.text: Brasília was built to promote settlement and development of Brazil's interior; the government began moving there from Rio de Janeiro on 21 April 1960.

Lúcio Costa's plan for Brasília, often compared to an airplane or a bird, has a straight Monumental Axis of government buildings and a curved Highway Axis of homes; Oscar Niemeyer designed its landmark buildings.
UNESCO listed Brasília as World Heritage in 1987 for its unique plan and architecture; critics attacked its cost and architecture, and Simone de Beauvoir found its housing districts sterile.

title: Cerdà's Eixample
description: Barcelona's walls came down and Cerdà's chamfered grid, meant to hold gardens, spread over the old field of fire.

facts.text: Barcelona's Eixample was built on open land that had been left clear to give a field of fire from the city walls.
In 1859, the engineer Ildefons Cerdà drew up a grid plan to extend Barcelona beyond its old walls, and it won royal approval.
Cerdà cut the corners of his blocks at 45 degrees so traffic could see along the crossing streets, which gives every crossing a small open space.
Cerdà's blocks were meant to leave open space and gardens in the middle of each block.
The plan was not fully carried out: within 30 years the open areas had been built over and building density tripled.
Cerdà is credited with inventing the word urbanization, which he set out in his General Theory of Urbanization (1867).

title: The Passive House
description: A Passive House keeps heat in with insulation, good windows and airtightness; the first was finished in Darmstadt in 1991.

facts.text: The world's first Passive House, a row of four homes in Darmstadt-Kranichstein, Germany, was finished in 1991; Wolfgang Feist's family was one of the four households.

The Passive House Institute lists five principles: very good thermal insulation, highly energy-efficient windows, airtightness, no thermal bridges, and ventilation with heat recovery; such buildings need very little heating energy.
The Darmstadt pioneers had triple-glazed windows specially made for the project and fitted four ventilation units with heat recovery.

title: Passive solar design
description: Passive solar design uses a building's windows, walls and floors to collect winter sun, store its heat and shade out summer sun.

facts.text: Passive solar design uses windows, walls and floors to collect, store and distribute the sun's heat; the US Department of Energy advises windows facing within 30 degrees of true south.
Passive solar design lets in the sun's low winter rays and deflects its high summer rays; roof overhangs can shade windows in summer, and thermal mass in floors and walls stores the heat.

title: Heat recovery ventilation
description: A heat recovery ventilator swaps stale air for fresh air through a heat exchanger, so the outgoing air warms the incoming air in winter.

facts.text: A heat recovery ventilator passes outgoing stale air and incoming fresh air through a heat exchanger, where heat moves from the warmer stream to the cooler one: warming incoming air in winter and cooling it in summer.

title: Green roofs
description: A green roof is a planted layer on a rooftop; light extensive roofs have a few inches of growing medium, while heavier intensive roofs can hold parks and trees.

facts.text: A green roof is a vegetative layer grown on a rooftop. Extensive green roofs use hardy plants in 2 to 4 inches of growing medium, are lightweight and need little maintenance; intensive ones can be parks with trees and need more structural support because they are heavier.
Green roofs have cooler surfaces than conventional roofs and can reduce and filter stormwater runoff.

title: Patrick Blanc's soil-free living walls
description: Botanist Patrick Blanc grows vertical gardens with no soil: roots grip felt on a PVC sheet on a metal frame, fed with water from the top.

facts.text: The botanist Patrick Blanc's Vertical Garden has three parts: a metal frame, a 1 cm PVC sheet and a polyamide felt; roots grow on and inside the felt, watered from the top with added nutrients.
With no soil, Blanc's whole Vertical Garden, plants and frame included, weighs under 30 kg per square metre, so it can go on any wall.
Patrick Blanc's vertical garden at the Quai Branly museum in Paris was completed in 2004.

title: Milan's Vertical Forest
description: Bosco Verticale in Milan holds 800 trees on its balconies; wind tunnel tests, safety cables and steel cages keep them in place.

facts.text: Stefano Boeri's Vertical Forest (Bosco Verticale) in Milan, two residential towers built from 2007 to 2014, holds 800 trees on its balconies, greenery equal to about five hectares of parkland.

Arup ran two wind tunnel test campaigns for Bosco Verticale's trees; medium and large trees have safety cables, and the largest trees in the windiest spots have steel cages restraining their root-balls.

title: Ascent: a timber high-rise
description: Milwaukee's 25-story Ascent, certified by CTBUH in 2022 as the tallest timber building, pairs mass timber with a concrete base and cores.

facts.text: In 2022 the Council on Tall Buildings and Urban Habitat (CTBUH) certified Ascent in Milwaukee, 25 stories and 86.6 m tall, as the world's tallest timber building.
Ascent has a concrete base and concrete elevator and stair shafts; 19 of its 25 stories are mass timber, cross-laminated timber (CLT) and glulam.
The USDA Forest Products Laboratory worked with Ascent's design team to evaluate how a three-hour fire would affect its glulam columns.

title: Cross-laminated timber
description: CLT panels are boards stacked in crossing layers and glued, which makes them stable, strong and stiff in both directions; they appeared in the early 1990s.

facts.text: Cross-laminated timber (CLT) panels are layers of lumber boards stacked crosswise, typically at 90 degrees, and glued together, with at least three layers; CLT was introduced in the early 1990s in Austria and Germany.
Cross-laminating gives CLT dimensional stability and strength and stiffness in both directions, so it can make wide, long floor slabs and walls.

title: How thick timber survives fire
description: Big timbers char on the outside; the char insulates the wood inside, which burns slowly and predictably, so the member keeps carrying load.

facts.text: Wood exposed to fire forms an insulating layer of char that slows further damage; in a standard fire test, wood chars at an average of about 0.6 mm per minute.
A wooden member's load-carrying capacity depends on its cross-section, so how much of it chars is the main factor in how long it lasts in a fire; thick timbers keep much of their strength.

title: The Eindhoven printed house
description: In 2021 the first Dutch 3D-printed concrete home got its tenants: 24 printed elements set on a foundation.

facts.text: On 30 April 2021 the first tenants of the Netherlands' first 3D-printed concrete house, in Eindhoven, received the key; the boulder-shaped home meets all the country's building requirements.
The Eindhoven house is made of 24 concrete elements printed layer by layer at a plant, trucked to the site and placed on a foundation.

title: Printing without formwork
description: Formwork is the temporary mold for wet concrete and a big share of its cost; a concrete printer extrudes walls layer by layer with no formwork.

facts.text: Formwork is the temporary structure that holds fluid concrete in its shape until it hardens; it accounts for more than half the resources needed for concrete structures.
Concrete 3D printing builds walls by extruding concrete through a nozzle layer by layer from a digital design, which eliminates the need for formwork.

title: Buildability of printed concrete
description: Printing concrete must flow through the nozzle, then hold the weight of the layers above without sagging.

facts.text: Concrete for 3D printing must flow well enough to be extruded through the nozzle, yet be strong enough to support the weight of the layers printed on top without deforming: its buildability.

title: Reinforcing printed concrete
description: Steel reinforcement has to cross the printed layers, which the nozzle's path makes hard; the joints between layers are also weak points.

facts.text: Without reinforcement, printed concrete lacks tensile strength, but the layer-by-layer process makes conventional steel reinforcement hard to add, and the joints between layers weaken printed structures compared with cast concrete.

title: Maasbommel's amphibious houses
description: At Maasbommel, 32 amphibious and 14 floating houses rise with the river on mooring posts; in 2011 they floated as designed.

facts.text: At Maasbommel in the Netherlands, 32 amphibious houses and 14 floating houses were built in 2004-2005 outside the river dikes.
In 2011 the River Maas rose high enough for Maasbommel's amphibious houses to float for the first time, and no problems were found.
Maasbommel's amphibious homes rest on concrete foundations and float when the river rises; its floating homes are a concrete barge with a relatively light timber frame on top.
Maasbommel's houses are moored on steel posts that let them rise and fall up to 5.5 m, with flexible pipes carrying their connections.

title: Why a concrete house floats
description: A floating building sinks until the water it pushes aside weighs as much as it does; a hollow concrete base displaces enough water to float.

facts.text: A floating object sinks until the water it displaces weighs as much as it does, and sinks deeper when it is loaded; the upward buoyant force equals the weight of the water displaced.
A lump of clay sinks, but the same clay shaped into a boat floats; steel ships float for the same reason.
Each Maasbommel amphibious house stands on a large, hollow concrete cube, moored on huge steel pipes.

title: Why the Moon is hard to build on
description: The Moon has almost no atmosphere, so no shield from radiation or meteoroids, huge temperature swings and one-sixth gravity.

facts.text: The Moon's very thin atmosphere gives no protection from the Sun's radiation or meteoroid impacts; its surface reaches about 127 C in full sunlight and about -173 C in darkness (a swing of about 300 degrees), and its gravity is one-sixth of Earth's.

title: The inside-out lunar building
description: A pressurized Moon habitat is pushed outward by the air inside, so it is mainly in tension, unlike buildings on Earth.

facts.text: Because the Moon has no atmosphere, a habitat holding Earth-level air pressure feels outward pressure several orders of magnitude greater than ordinary gravity and weather loads on Earth buildings.
A pressurized habitat on the Moon is mainly in tension, instead of the compression gravity causes in buildings on Earth.
Regolith is loose, broken soil and rock; a thick outer layer of it on a lunar habitat could dampen temperature swings and shield against radiation.

title: ESA's printed lunar base study
description: In 2013 ESA and Foster + Partners studied a lunar base: an inflatable dome under a robot-printed regolith shell shaped as a catenary dome.

facts.text: In 2013 ESA and partners including Foster + Partners studied 3D printing a lunar base from regolith: an inflatable, pressurized dome sheltering astronauts, covered by a robot-printed regolith shell.
The ESA study's shell was a weight-bearing catenary dome with hollow, closed-cell walls like bird bones, and the team printed a 1.5-tonne building block as a demonstration.
The curve a chain makes when it hangs freely from two points is called a catenary; turned upside down, it gives an arch.

title: Restore or protect?
description: Viollet-le-Duc restored buildings and often added his own designs; William Morris's SPAB (1877) asked for protection and daily care instead.

facts.text: Eugene Viollet-le-Duc and Jean-Baptiste Lassus were appointed in 1844 to restore Notre-Dame de Paris; Viollet-le-Duc aimed to restore in the original style but often added entirely new elements of his own design.
Twentieth-century archaeologists and restorers severely criticized Viollet-le-Duc's added structures posing as restorations, because they often destroyed or obscured the original form.

The Society for the Protection of Ancient Buildings' 1877 manifesto, by William Morris, Philip Webb and others, called on people to 'put Protection in the place of Restoration, to stave off decay by daily care'.

title: Rebuilding Notre-Dame's spire
description: After the 2019 fire, Notre-Dame's spire was rebuilt as an exact replica of Viollet-le-Duc's 1859 spire, and the cathedral reopened in December 2024.

facts.text: The fire at Notre-Dame de Paris on 15 April 2019 destroyed most of the roof, Viollet-le-Duc's 19th-century spire and some of the rib vaulting.

Notre-Dame's new timber spire, topped by a metal cross and 96 m high, is an exact replica of the one Viollet-le-Duc built in 1859; carpenters cut and carved it in their workshops and assembled it piece by piece in the cathedral, which reopened in December 2024.

title: A power station turned gallery
description: Tate Modern reused Giles Gilbert Scott's Bankside Power Station, closed in 1981, as an art museum opened in 2000.

facts.text: Giles Gilbert Scott's Bankside Power Station in London opened in 1962 and shut down in 1981; after its machinery was removed, Herzog & de Meuron converted it, and it opened as Tate Modern on 11 May 2000, with its Turbine Hall used for giant artworks.

title: The curb cut
description: Curb cuts, pushed for by disabled activists (Berkeley, 1972), turned out to help parents, workers and travelers too.

facts.text: Pressed by disabled activists, Berkeley installed its first official curb cut at an intersection on Telegraph Avenue in 1972; the first curb cuts had appeared in Kalamazoo, Michigan, in 1945.
Curb cuts turned out to help far more than wheelchair users: parents pushing strollers, workers pushing heavy carts and travelers wheeling luggage use them too.

title: Universal design
description: Universal design, championed by Ronald Mace, means designing for all people from the start, without special adaptations.

facts.text: NC State's Center for Universal Design, founded in 1989 and guided by the architect Ronald Mace, who coined the term, defines universal design as design usable by all people, to the greatest extent possible, without the need for adaptation or specialized design.

Seven Principles of Universal Design were published in 1997; the first, Equitable Use, asks for the same means of use for all users, identical whenever possible, and avoiding segregating or stigmatizing anyone.

title: The 1:12 ramp
description: US accessibility standards cap ramp slopes at 1:12: every inch of rise needs at least 12 inches of run.

facts.text: The 2010 ADA Standards for Accessible Design require ramp runs to have a running slope no steeper than 1:12, one unit of rise for every 12 of run.

title: Reading a building
description: Historic England's method: take a quick overview of functions and phases first, then read clues like masonry joints and blocked openings.

facts.text: Historic England advises starting an investigation of a building with a quick overview, identifying its functions and main phases, to see it as a functioning whole; investigation asks what it shows of its origins, form, function, date and development.
Historic England's guide lists clues to a building's phases and date: evidence of phasing such as masonry joints, architectural styles, plan elements, decorative schemes, and fixtures and fittings.
Historic England's guide says plans should record structural features such as blocked doorways, windows and fireplaces, and masonry joints.
